docs.title: Individual EMS Awareness — The Soldier's Electromagnetic Discipline
docs.text: "Every transmission exposes a signature vulnerable to enemy exploitation. Control your emissions." — SATTL, Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations for Military Service Members

docs.title: The Soldier as Emitter
docs.text:
Every soldier carries devices that emit electromagnetic energy. Radios, GPS receivers, smartphones, smartwatches, fitness trackers, and even Bluetooth earpieces all create detectable signatures. The enemy uses these signatures to locate, identify, and target friendly forces.

This page covers the individual discipline every soldier must practise to survive in the electromagnetic domain.

docs.title: How the Enemy Uses the EMS
docs.text: Adversaries employ electronic support (ES) systems to: - Detect your emissions. Every radio transmission, GPS signal, and Wi-Fi connection can be detected from kilometres away. - Identify your unit. Different units use different frequencies and equipment. The enemy builds an electronic order of battle from your emissions. - Locate your position. Direction-finding systems can pinpoint your transmitter's location. - Target your position. Once located, your position can be struck with artillery, air attack, or electronic attack.

docs.title: Real-World Examples
docs.text:
• Ukraine 2014. Russian forces targeted Ukrainian artillery battalions using location data from soldiers' personal smartphones.
  • Modern conflicts. Adversaries use commercially available equipment to detect and exploit friendly emissions. Cheap drones with RF sensors can locate infantry positions.

docs.title: Principles of EMCON
docs.text:
Emission control is the management of electromagnetic emissions to avoid enemy detection. Key principles:

  1. Minimum power. Use the lowest power setting necessary for communications. Higher power increases detection range.

  2. Transmission brevity. Keep radio calls short. Use brevity codes and prowords. Long transmissions are easier to detect and locate.

  3. Directional antennas. Use directional antennas when possible. They focus the signal toward the intended receiver and reduce exposure to enemy sensors.

  4. Terrain masking. Position yourself behind hills or buildings to shield transmissions from enemy direction-finding systems.

  5. Vary patterns. Change transmission times and frequencies. Predictable patterns make enemy collection easier.

  6. Lower antennas. Reduce antenna height. Lower antennas reduce detection range while maintaining local communications.

docs.title: Personal Devices
docs.text:
Personal electronic devices are a major vulnerability: - Smartphones continuously transmit and can reveal your location. - Smartwatches and fitness trackers emit Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals. - Bluetooth earpieces create detectable signatures.

Leave personal devices behind when deploying. If you must carry them, disable all wireless functions and remove the battery if possible.

docs.title: Radio Procedures
docs.text:
• Use frequency-hopping radios (SINCGARS) when available. They hop across frequencies at 100 hops per second, making interception and jamming difficult.
  • Use encrypted communications when available.
  • Avoid plain-language transmissions. Use codes and brevity lists.
  • Do not transmit unnecessary information. Every transmission is a risk.

docs.title: When Jammed
docs.text: If you experience jamming: - Do not increase power immediately. This may reveal your position further. - Switch to an alternate frequency. - Use directional antennas. - Report the jamming to higher headquarters. - Switch to alternate means of communication (messengers, wire lines, visual signals).

docs.title: The GPS Threat
docs.text: GPS jamming and spoofing are common in modern conflicts. Adversaries can: - Jam GPS signals, denying your ability to navigate. - Spoof GPS signals, providing false position data that causes weapons to miss or forces to move to wrong locations.

docs.title: Alternative Navigation
docs.text: When GPS is denied: - Use terrain association. Match map contours to ground features. - Use dead reckoning. Track direction and distance from a known point. - Use celestial navigation (compass and stars) when possible. - Use inertial navigation systems if available. - Pre-plan routes with multiple navigation methods.

docs.title: Before Operations
docs.text:
• Remove or disable personal electronic devices.
  • Check all equipment for proper shielding.
  • Verify encryption settings on radios.
  • Brief soldiers on EMCON procedures.
  • Establish emission control conditions (EMCON levels).

docs.title: During Operations
docs.text:
• Monitor for jamming or interference.
  • Report any unusual electromagnetic activity.
  • Maintain emission discipline at all times.
  • Use visual and acoustic signals when possible to reduce radio traffic.

docs.title: After Operations
docs.text:
• Report any electromagnetic incidents.
  • Update electronic threat databases.
  • Refine EMCON procedures based on lessons learned.

docs.title: Tactical EMS Operations — Platoon and Company Integration
docs.text: "The goal of tactical spectrum operations is to control the electromagnetic spectrum so that it serves the needs of friendly forces while denying use to the enemy." — FM 6-02.70, Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations

docs.title: EMS at the Tactical Edge
docs.text:
At platoon and company level, the electromagnetic spectrum (EMS) is both an enabler and a vulnerability. You depend on it for communications, navigation, and target acquisition. The enemy depends on it for the same purposes. Whoever controls the EMS at the tactical edge gains the advantage.

This page covers the integration of EMS operations at platoon and company level. It focuses on how small unit commanders manage their electromagnetic signature, coordinate with electronic warfare assets, and operate in contested spectrum environments.

docs.title: Know Your Signature
docs.text:
Every piece of equipment in your platoon emits electromagnetic energy: - Radios (voice and data) - GPS receivers - Counter-RCIED devices - Unmanned aerial systems (UAS) - Battle command systems - Personal electronic devices (phones, tablets)

Make an inventory. Know what your platoon emits. Understand which systems are essential and which are optional. The more you emit, the easier you are to detect.

docs.title: Emission Control
docs.text: As a platoon commander, you set the emission control posture for your platoon. Consider: - What is the threat? If the enemy has electronic warfare capabilities, emissions must be tightly controlled. - What is the mission? Some missions require continuous communications. Others require radio silence. - What is the higher headquarters' EMCON posture? Ensure your platoon complies with battalion guidance.

docs.title: Coordinate with the Battalion EW Noncommissioned Officer
docs.text: At battalion level, an EW NCO coordinates electronic warfare operations. At platoon level, you work with the EW NCO to: - Request electronic warfare support (direction finding, jamming). - Report enemy electronic emissions. - Coordinate frequency assignments. - Troubleshoot interference problems.

docs.title: The Company Executive Officer's Role
docs.text: The company executive officer (XO) typically coordinates spectrum management matters. Responsibilities include: - Maintaining the frequency plan. Know what frequencies are assigned to each platoon. - Deconflicting frequencies. Prevent platoons from interfering with each other. - Reporting interference. Document and report any electromagnetic interference to the battalion signal officer (S6). - Distributing the signal operating instructions (SOI). Ensure all platoon leaders have the current SOI extract.

docs.title: The Company-Level CEMA Working Group
docs.text: At company level, a formal CEMA working group may not exist. However, the commander should designate someone (often the XO or a senior NCO) to: - Track friendly and enemy electromagnetic emissions. - Coordinate with the battalion CEMA section. - Advise the commander on electromagnetic protection measures.

docs.title: What EW Can Do for You
docs.text: Electronic warfare assets at brigade and battalion level can provide: - Electronic support (ES). Detect and locate enemy emitters (radios, radars, cell phones). - Electronic attack (EA). Jam enemy communications or radar. - Electronic protection (EP). Protect your systems from enemy jamming.

docs.title: Requesting EW Support
docs.text: To request EW support: 1. Identify the need. What enemy emitter are you targeting? What effect do you want? 2. Submit a request. Use the format specified in the operations order (often a spot report or a formal request through the CEMA section). 3. Provide location information. Give grid references and descriptions of the target area. 4. Coordinate timing. Specify when the effect is needed.

docs.title: Operating with Attached EW Assets
docs.text: If an EW team is attached to your platoon or company: - Protect the team. EW teams carry sensitive equipment and are high-value targets. - Provide information. Share what you know about enemy emissions and communications. - Coordinate movement. EW teams may need to move to optimal positions for sensing or jamming. - Respect their constraints. EW operations require careful coordination to avoid fratricide (jamming friendly systems).

docs.title: The Threat
docs.text: GPS jamming is common in modern conflicts. At platoon level, GPS denial affects: - Navigation. - Position reporting. - Target acquisition (some weapons systems rely on GPS). - Time synchronization for communications.

docs.title: Countermeasures
docs.text:
• Use terrain association and dead reckoning as primary navigation methods.
  • Pre-plan routes with multiple navigation methods.
  • Use visual and acoustic signals for navigation in close terrain.
  • Report GPS denial immediately to higher headquarters.
  • Use alternative timing sources if GPS time is lost.

docs.title: Patrol Base Operations
docs.text: When occupying a patrol base: - Minimize emissions. Use wired communications if possible. - Use directional antennas to reduce signal exposure. - Control personal devices. Enforce a no-personal-devices policy. - Maintain EMCON discipline. Brief all soldiers on emission procedures.

docs.title: Movement
docs.text: During movement: - Use proper radio procedures. Keep transmissions short and infrequent. - Vary routes and timing. Predictable patterns aid enemy collection. - Maintain communications silence when required by the operations order. - Use visual signals when radio silence is in effect.

docs.title: Attack and Defense
docs.text:
During offensive operations: - Jam enemy communications if EW support is available. - Use deception. False radio traffic can mislead the enemy about your intentions. - Maintain communications security. Do not transmit sensitive information in the clear.

During defensive operations: - Use the EMS to detect enemy approaches. Report enemy radio traffic. - Prepare for enemy jamming. Have alternate communication plans. - Protect friendly emitters. Use terrain masking and directional antennas.

docs.title: Landward Domain — Nature and Military Relevance
docs.text:
"The land is where people live and compete, where most wars are fought and decided, and where peace is usually concluded." — Joint Doctrine Publication 0-20, UK Land Power

The landward domain is the physical environment where human beings live, work, and fight. It is the only domain permanently inhabited by people. This fundamental truth shapes every aspect of land warfare and distinguishes the land domain from all others.

This page examines the nature of the land domain, its enduring characteristics, and its centrality to military operations.

docs.title: The Nature of the Land Domain
The Human Domain
docs.text:
The land domain is defined by the permanent presence of people. Unlike the air, maritime, space, or cyber domains, the land environment is home to the vast majority of the world's population. This has profound implications for military operations.

Land operations are conducted among and against people. Civilians are present in every theatre of operations. Their presence complicates every aspect of warfare — from targeting to logistics to information operations. Land forces must account for the civilian presence in every plan and every action.

The roots of conflict are usually found on land. People fight for things they value: their lives, their property, their resources, their beliefs, their systems of governance. These things exist on land. Air and maritime power can influence events on land, but only land forces can fully control the land environment.

docs.title: The Physical Domain
docs.text:
The land domain is the most physically complex of all operational domains. Terrain varies enormously — from open plains to dense jungle, from mountains to deserts to urban sprawl. Each type of terrain imposes different constraints on movement, observation, and fire.

Weather and climate further complicate the land environment. Rain, snow, heat, cold, fog, and wind all affect operations. A sandstorm can halt a mechanised advance. Winter can immobilise an army. Monsoon rains can render roads impassable.

This physical complexity makes land operations inherently uncertain. No two pieces of terrain are alike. No two battles are fought under identical conditions. Land forces must adapt constantly to the physical environment.

docs.title: The Close Combat Domain
docs.text:
Land warfare is unique in its intimacy. Combatants routinely come face-to-face with one another. Close combat — direct-fire fighting at close range — is the defining characteristic of land operations.

Other domains fight at range. Aircraft engage targets from altitude. Ships engage targets over the horizon. Cyber operators engage targets remotely. Land forces, by contrast, must often close with the enemy and destroy or capture them at close range.

This proximity makes land warfare the most psychologically demanding form of combat. Soldiers must overcome the natural resistance to killing at close quarters. Training, leadership, and unit cohesion are the factors that enable soldiers to fight in close combat.

docs.title: Enduring Characteristics of the Land Domain
1. Permanence
docs.text:
Land operations involve the seizure and control of terrain. With control of terrain comes control of populations and their activities. Those whose behaviour must be changed are resident on land and must ultimately be controlled there.

The effects of land operations are enduring. A city seized remains seized. A population controlled remains controlled. This permanence gives land power its strategic significance. Air strikes can destroy, but only land forces can hold ground.

docs.title: 2. Persistence
docs.text:
Land forces can maintain a presence in an area for extended periods. This persistence allows land forces to broaden and deepen their understanding of the local environment. It enables sustained engagement with the population and the gradual establishment of security.

Persistence is a unique attribute of land forces. Air and maritime forces can project power, but they cannot maintain a continuous presence in the same way. Land forces live among the people and operate in the same environment day after day.

docs.title: 3. Adaptability
docs.text:
Land forces are inherently adaptable. They consist largely of organised groups with the ability to conduct a wide range of military and non-military tasks. Land forces can fight, engage, secure, and support — often simultaneously.

This adaptability gives land power its broad strategic utility. The same force that conducts combat operations can also conduct stability operations, humanitarian assistance, and engagement tasks. No other domain offers this range of capabilities.

docs.title: 4. Complexity
docs.text:
The land environment is the most complex operational domain. Terrain, weather, civilians, infrastructure, and human geography all interact to create an environment of enormous complexity.

This complexity generates friction — the accumulation of small difficulties, errors, and uncertainties that make war difficult. Clausewitz observed that "everything in war is very simple, but the simplest thing is difficult." This is especially true on land.

docs.title: 5. Lethality
docs.text:
Large-scale ground combat is the most lethal form of warfare. The combination of direct and indirect fires, the proximity of combatants, and the complexity of the environment produce high casualty rates.

Modern land warfare is increasingly lethal. Precision-guided munitions, advanced sensors, and improved fire coordination have increased the destructiveness of land operations. Urban terrain, while providing cover, also creates kill zones and ambush points.

docs.title: 6. Civilian Presence
docs.text:
Land operations affect civilians by disrupting routine life patterns and potentially placing them in harm's way. There are few uninhabited places in which land forces are likely to fight.

The civilian presence imposes legal, moral, and operational constraints. Land forces must comply with the law of armed conflict, minimise civilian casualties, and provide for the welfare of affected populations. These requirements complicate operations but are essential to maintaining legitimacy.

docs.title: 7. Combined Arms
docs.text:
Land operations require the synchronised and simultaneous application of multiple capabilities — infantry, armour, artillery, engineers, aviation, and supporting arms. No single arm can achieve success alone.

Combined arms is the fundamental approach to land warfare. It reinforces strengths and compensates for weaknesses. It imposes dilemmas on opponents by confronting them with multiple threats simultaneously.

docs.title: The Land Domain and Multi-Domain Operations
docs.text:
Modern land operations are inherently multi-domain. Land forces depend on capabilities from other domains: air support, maritime logistics, space-based communications and positioning, cyber defence, and electromagnetic spectrum management.

At the same time, land forces enable operations in other domains. Ground-based air defence protects airspace. Land-based electronic warfare degrades enemy communications. Land forces seize and hold terrain that enables air and maritime operations.

This mutual interdependence reflects the reality that all operations have multi-domain components. The land domain is not isolated. It is the foundation upon which multi-domain operations are built.

docs.title: Implications for Military Operations
docs.text:
The land domain has direct implications at every level of war:

  • Strategic: Wars are ultimately decided on land. The ability to prevail in ground combat is the decisive factor in breaking an enemy's will.

  • Operational: Campaigns are designed to achieve objectives on land. The arrangement of battles and major operations to seize key terrain and destroy enemy forces is the essence of operational art.

  • Tactical: Battles and engagements are fought at specific locations and times. The coordination of combined arms in the attack or defence is the essence of tactics.

docs.title: Battalion Staff Landward Operations — The Cognitive Architecture of Command
docs.text:
"The battle staff is that element within the organisation which helps the commander create and refine the battlefield image." — FM 6-0, Commander and Staff Organization and Operations

The battalion commander operates at the tactical level where multiple companies are coordinated in the landward domain. The battalion staff — S1 (personnel), S2 (intelligence), S3 (operations), S4 (logistics), and supporting cells — enables the commander to visualise the battlespace, make decisions, and synchronise the actions of subordinate units.

This page discusses the landward domain at the battalion staff level, relevant to majors, captains, and staff officers.

docs.title: The Battalion Staff's Spatial Problem
docs.text: The battalion staff must maintain a common operating picture (COP) of the landward battlespace. This requires the integration of information from multiple sources: company reports, intelligence feeds, reconnaissance assets, and adjacent units.

docs.title: Key Spatial Functions
docs.text:
• Intelligence preparation of the battlefield (IPB): The S2, supported by the S3, analyses the terrain and enemy to produce a detailed picture of the battlespace. IPB identifies key terrain, enemy avenues of approach, and likely enemy positions.

  • Common operating picture: The staff maintains a shared visual representation of the landward battlespace. The COP shows the positions of friendly and enemy units, control measures, and key terrain.

  • Control measures: The staff establishes control measures — boundaries, phase lines, objectives, and fire support coordination measures — that define the spatial framework for operations.

  • Terrain management: The staff allocates terrain to subordinate units based on the commander's intent. Each company is assigned an area of operations that provides the space it needs to accomplish its mission.

docs.title: The Battalion Staff's Temporal Problem
docs.text: The battalion staff manages time through the battle rhythm — the routine cycle of meetings, reports, and orders that synchronises the battalion's operations.

docs.title: Key Temporal Functions
docs.text:
• Synchronisation: The S3 coordinates the actions of companies, supporting weapons, and adjacent units to produce maximum combined effect at the right time.

  • Decision cycle management: The staff manages the commander's decision cycle. The commander makes decisions at key points in the operation. The staff ensures that the commander has the information needed to make those decisions on time.

  • Reporting: The staff establishes reporting requirements that provide the commander with timely information without overwhelming the staff with unnecessary data.

  • Planning horizons: The staff manages multiple planning horizons simultaneously. Current operations are executed. Near-future operations are planned. Far-future operations are conceptualised.

docs.title: The Land Battle at Battalion Level
docs.text: The battalion attacks and defends as a combined arms team. The battalion commander integrates infantry, armour, artillery, engineers, aviation, and supporting arms to achieve the mission.

docs.title: The Battalion Attack
docs.text:
The battalion attack is a complex combined arms operation. The staff must:

  1. Plan: Develop a scheme of manoeuvre that places companies on objectives at the right time. Coordinate supporting fires. Establish control measures. Issue orders.

  2. Prepare: Move companies to the line of departure. Coordinate with adjacent units. Brief company commanders. Ensure all units understand the plan.

  3. Execute: Control the battalion's movement. Adjust the plan as the situation changes. Commit reserves at the right time and place.

  4. Consolidate: Secure objectives. Reorganise the battalion. Prepare for counterattack.

docs.title: The Battalion Defence
docs.text:
The battalion defence is a complex combined arms operation. The staff must:

  1. Plan: Develop a defensive scheme that destroys the enemy before they reach the battalion's positions. Coordinate direct and indirect fires. Establish control measures. Issue orders.

  2. Prepare: Construct defences. Clear fields of fire. Lay mines and obstacles. Rehearse the defence.

  3. Execute: Control the defence. Call for indirect fire. Commit reserves at the decisive moment.

  4. Counterattack: Conduct counterattacks to retake lost terrain or exploit enemy weaknesses.

docs.title: Combined Arms at the Battalion Level
docs.text:
Combined arms at the battalion level requires the integration of multiple capabilities:

  • Infantry: The primary arm. Holds ground, closes with the enemy, operates in any terrain.

  • Armour: Mobile protected firepower. Most effective in open terrain.

  • Artillery: Indirect fire support. Shapes the battlefield, suppresses the enemy, provides illumination.

  • Engineers: Mobility and counter-mobility. Breach obstacles, clear minefields, construct defences.

  • Aviation: Reconnaissance, fire support, mobility. Attack helicopters destroy armour. Transport helicopters insert troops.

  • Air defence: Protection from air and missile threats.

  • Electronic warfare: Degrades enemy communications and sensors.

The battalion staff coordinates these capabilities to produce effects greater than the sum of their parts.

docs.title: The S2/S3 Relationship
docs.text:
The S2 (intelligence) and S3 (operations) relationship is the core of the battalion staff's landward operations. The S2 provides the spatial picture — where is the enemy, what is the terrain, what are the enemy's likely courses of action. The S3 provides the temporal picture — when will actions occur, how long will they take, what is the sequence of events.

Together, the S2 and S3 enable the commander to visualise the landward battlespace in four dimensions: three of space and one of time.

docs.title: Case Study — Battle of Leuctra (371 BC): The Shattering of Spartan Supremacy
docs.text:
"The Theban left wing, fifty shields deep, struck the Spartan line at its strongest point, and the strongest point gave way." — Front Line Stories

This case study examines the Battle of Leuctra, fought in 371 BC between a Theban-led Boeotian force and a Spartan-led Peloponnesian alliance. The battle is one of the most tactically innovative engagements in military history and demonstrates several enduring principles of land warfare.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
For over two centuries, Sparta had been the dominant military power in Greece. The Spartan hoplite, the Spartiatae, was considered the finest heavy infantry in the Greek world. No Spartan army had lost a pitched land battle in living memory.

Thebes, the chief city of Boeotia, had long existed in Sparta's shadow. But by 371 BC, under the leadership of Epaminondas and Pelopidas, Thebes had developed a new approach to warfare that would shatter Spartan supremacy in a single afternoon.

docs.title: Spartan Alliance
docs.text:
The Spartan-led alliance numbered approximately 10,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry. The elite Spartiate hoplites formed the right wing — the position of honour in Greek warfare. King Cleombrotus commanded the Spartan forces personally.

The Spartan cavalry was of poor quality. Wealthier Spartans sent horses and hired substitutes to ride them, producing undertrained riders on unfamiliar mounts.

docs.title: Theban-Boeotian Force
docs.text:
The Theban-Boeotian force numbered approximately 6,000 to 7,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry. The Theban cavalry was well-trained and fighting on home ground.

Epaminondas commanded the Theban forces. He had spent years developing new tactical concepts that broke from the conventional Greek approach to warfare.

docs.title: Conventional Greek Battle
docs.text:
Greek hoplite warfare was essentially a pushing contest between two rectangular formations. Each formation deployed in a line, typically eight to twelve ranks deep. The right wing was the position of honour, where the best troops were placed. The tendency was for the stronger right wing to push back the weaker enemy left, then wheel inward to roll up the enemy line.

This symmetrical approach had produced many battles but few decisive results. The stronger right wing usually prevailed, but the enemy could withdraw in good order.

docs.title: Epaminondas's Innovation
docs.text: Epaminondas rejected the symmetrical approach. His innovation had three elements:

docs.title: 1. Concentration on the Decisive Wing
docs.text:
Epaminondas stacked the Theban left wing to an unprecedented depth of fifty ranks. This was twice the depth of any previous Greek formation. The elite Sacred Band, under Pelopidas, formed the cutting edge of this mass.

The concentration was deliberate. Epaminondas intended to strike the Spartan right wing — the strongest point of the enemy line — with overwhelming force.

docs.title: 2. The Refused Flank
docs.text:
Epaminondas refused the Theban right wing. He ordered the weaker Boeotian contingents on the right to hold back and avoid engagement. This oblique approach meant the Theban right would not clash with the Spartan left and collapse, as it likely would have done on conventional terms.

The refused flank is one of the most important tactical innovations in military history. It allows a commander to concentrate overwhelming force at a decisive point while minimising risk elsewhere.

docs.title: 3. Cavalry as a Disruptive Force
docs.text: The Theban cavalry attacked early in the engagement and drove off the Spartan cavalry. The fleeing Spartan cavalry disrupted the Spartan infantry formations before the main infantry clash. This disruption weakened the Spartan right wing at the critical moment.

docs.title: The Battle
docs.text:
The decisive engagement lasted approximately thirty minutes. The sequence was:

  1. Cavalry engagement: The Theban cavalry routed the Spartan cavalry, which fled back into the Spartan infantry lines, disrupting their formation.

  2. Infantry clash: The Theban left wing, fifty ranks deep, struck the Spartan right wing. The Spartan formation, disrupted by its own cavalry and overwhelmed by the depth of the Theban formation, buckled.

  3. Death of Cleombrotus: King Cleombrotus was killed in the fighting. The loss of the king and the elite Spartiates broke the Spartan will to fight.

  4. Rout: The Spartan right wing collapsed. The Spartan left wing, which had not been heavily engaged, withdrew in good order. But the battle was lost.

docs.title: Aftermath
docs.text:
The battle resulted in the death of approximately 400 Spartiate citizens — a catastrophic proportion of the remaining Spartiate military class. The political and strategic consequences rippled across the Greek world within months:

  • Spartan hegemony over the Peloponnesian League collapsed
  • Arcadia moved toward confederation
  • Epaminondas's subsequent campaigns freed the Messenian helots
  • Sparta's capacity to project military power was permanently curtailed

docs.title: 1. Concentration at the Decisive Point
docs.text:
Epaminondas did not attempt to defeat the entire Spartan army. He concentrated overwhelming force at a single point — the Spartan right wing — and destroyed it. The rest of the Spartan army, deprived of its command and its best troops, could not fight on.

This is the principle of concentration applied with precision. The decisive point is not always the weakest point. Sometimes it is the strongest point, because destroying the enemy's greatest strength shatters their will to resist.

docs.title: 2. The Refused Flank
docs.text:
The refused flank allows a commander to mass force at the decisive point without risking defeat elsewhere. It is an economy of force measure that accepts risk in one area to achieve overwhelming advantage in another.

The refused flank has been used by commanders throughout history. Napoleon used it at Austerlitz. The Germans used it in the Schlieffen Plan. It remains a valid approach in modern operations.

docs.title: 3. Combined Arms
docs.text: Epaminondas integrated cavalry and infantry to produce an effect greater than either arm could achieve alone. The cavalry disrupted the Spartan formation before the infantry struck. This is the essence of combined arms.

docs.title: 4. Moral Factors Decide
docs.text:
The death of Cleombrotus and the loss of 400 Spartiates broke the Spartan will to fight. The physical destruction of the right wing was decisive not because of the numbers killed, but because of what it represented: the Spartan king and the finest warriors in Greece, destroyed by a Theban innovation.

This reflects the enduring truth that land warfare is fundamentally a clash of wills. Physical destruction matters because of its moral effect.

docs.title: 5. Tactical Innovation Prevails
docs.text:
Epaminondas broke the conventional wisdom of Greek warfare. The conventional wisdom said: deploy symmetrically, put your best troops on the right, push. Epaminondas said: concentrate overwhelmingly on the decisive wing, refuse the other wing, use cavalry to disrupt.

The conventional approach had produced stalemate. The innovative approach produced decision. This is a recurring theme in military history: those who innovate tactically defeat those who follow convention.

docs.title: Platoon Commander's Landward Operations — Manoeuvre and Combined Arms at the Tactical Level
docs.text:
"The platoon leader must have a relatively complete knowledge of the terrain, and he must know as much as possible about the enemy." — FM 3-21.8, Infantry Platoon and Squad

The platoon commander operates at the tactical level where intent is translated into action. The platoon commander receives the company commander's intent and must achieve it through the coordinated action of multiple sections. This requires mastery of manoeuvre and combined arms at a higher level than the section commander.

This page discusses the landward domain at the platoon and company level, relevant to lieutenants and captains.

docs.title: The Manoeuvrist Approach
docs.text:
The manoeuvrist approach is an indirect approach that applies strength against enemy vulnerabilities. It blends lethal and non-lethal actions to shape the enemy's understanding, undermine their will, and break their cohesion.

The manoeuvrist approach is suited to a small, professional force. It avoids attritional warfare — the grinding destruction of enemy forces through superior firepower. Instead, it seeks to dislocate and disintegrate the enemy through speed, surprise, and the concentration of force at the decisive point.

docs.title: Shaping the Enemy's Understanding
docs.text: The manoeuvrist approach seeks to shape what the enemy perceives. Deception, feints, and indirect approaches confuse the enemy about the location and timing of the main effort. The enemy is induced to make mistakes — to commit reserves to the wrong location, to expose flanks, or to hesitate at the critical moment.

docs.title: Breaking Cohesion
docs.text: The manoeuvrist approach seeks to break the enemy's cohesion — the ability of the enemy force to act as a unified whole. Cohesion is broken by creating multiple dilemmas simultaneously. The enemy is forced to choose between responding to one threat or another. Whichever choice the enemy makes, they become vulnerable to the other threat.

docs.title: Combined Arms at the Platoon Level
docs.text: Combined arms is the synchronised and simultaneous application of tactical forces and capabilities to create an effect greater than if each element was used separately. At the platoon level, combined arms means the integration of infantry, armour, artillery, engineers, and aviation.

docs.title: Infantry
docs.text: Infantry is the primary arm of land warfare. Infantry can operate in any terrain. Infantry can close with the enemy and destroy or capture them at close range. Infantry can hold ground against counterattack.

docs.title: Armour
docs.text: Armour provides mobile protected firepower. Tanks and infantry fighting vehicles can destroy enemy armour, suppress enemy positions, and break through enemy defences. Armour is most effective in open terrain where its mobility and firepower can be fully exploited.

docs.title: Artillery
docs.text: Artillery provides indirect fire support. Mortars and field guns can suppress the enemy, destroy enemy positions, and provide smoke and illumination. Artillery is the primary means of shaping the battlefield before the assault.

docs.title: Engineers
docs.text: Engineers provide mobility and counter-mobility. Engineers breach obstacles, clear minefields, and construct defences. Engineers enable the force to move through denied terrain and prevent the enemy from moving through key terrain.

docs.title: Aviation
docs.text: Aviation provides reconnaissance, fire support, and mobility. Attack helicopters can destroy enemy armour and suppress enemy positions. Transport helicopters can insert troops into denied terrain. Unmanned aerial systems provide real-time intelligence.

docs.title: The Platoon Attack
docs.text: The platoon attack is a combined arms operation. The platoon commander coordinates the actions of sections, supporting weapons, and adjacent units to achieve the objective.

docs.title: The Plan
docs.text:
The platoon commander develops a plan that includes:

  • Mission analysis: What is the mission? What are the key factors? What are the enemy's likely courses of action?

  • Scheme of manoeuvre: How will the platoon achieve the objective? What is the main effort? What is the supporting effort?

  • Fire support plan: How will supporting weapons support the attack? What are the targets? When will fires be lifted?

  • Coordinating instructions: What are the control measures? What are the rules of engagement? What is the timeline?

docs.title: The Preparation
docs.text:
The platoon commander prepares the platoon for the attack. Preparation includes:

  • Reconnaissance: The platoon commander conducts a reconnaissance of the objective and the routes to the objective.

  • Briefing: The platoon commander briefs section commanders on the plan. Every section commander must understand the mission, the scheme of manoeuvre, and the fire support plan.

  • Rehearsal: The platoon rehearses the attack. Rehearsals identify problems and build confidence.

docs.title: The Execution
docs.text: The platoon commander controls the attack through fire and movement. The platoon commander designates the main effort and coordinates supporting fires. The platoon commander adjusts the plan as the situation changes.

docs.title: Consolidation
docs.text: The platoon consolidates on the objective. Consolidation includes reorganising the platoon, redistributing ammunition, and preparing for counterattack. Consolidation is often neglected but is critical to holding ground.

docs.title: The Platoon Defence
docs.text: The platoon defence is a combined arms operation. The platoon commander positions sections to maximise firepower while minimising exposure. The platoon commander coordinates supporting weapons to destroy the enemy before they reach the platoon's positions.

docs.title: The Plan
docs.text:
The platoon commander develops a defensive plan that includes:

  • Security: Early warning of the enemy's approach. Observation posts and patrols.

  • Main battle area: The positions where the platoon will fight. Primary, alternate, and supplementary positions.

  • Fire support plan: The integration of direct and indirect fires. Target reference points. Final protective fires.

  • Reserve: A section held back to counterattack or reinforce.

docs.title: The Preparation
docs.text:
The platoon commander prepares the defence. Preparation includes:

  • Position construction: Fighting positions, trenches, and obstacles.

  • Fire planning: Clearing fields of fire. Assigning sectors of fire.

  • Rehearsal: Rehearsal of the defence, including the counterattack.

docs.title: The Execution
docs.text: The platoon commander controls the defence. The platoon commander calls for indirect fire. The platoon commander commits the reserve at the decisive moment.

docs.title: The Platoon Commander's Landward Problem
docs.text:
The platoon commander faces a complex landward problem. The platoon commander must simultaneously manoeuvre sections, coordinate supporting weapons, and maintain situational awareness. The platoon commander must be able to shift from offence to defence quickly and to adapt to the changing situation.

The platoon commander who masters combined arms and the manoeuvrist approach is the platoon commander who wins.

docs.title: Section Commander's Landward Operations — Reading Ground, Fighting, and Holding
docs.text:
"The section is the smallest military unit capable of independent tactical action." — ATP 3-21.8, Infantry Platoon and Squad

The section commander operates at the lowest level of military command. Decisions are immediate. The consequences are direct. The section commander must read the ground, fight the battle, and hold the ground — all simultaneously.

This page discusses the landward domain at the tactical level most relevant to junior leaders: the lance corporal and corporal commanding a fire team or section.

docs.title: Reading the Ground
docs.text: Terrain is the physical framework within which every engagement occurs. The section commander must read terrain quickly and accurately.

docs.title: Key Terrain Features
docs.text:
Terrain is analysed using the military mnemonic OCOKA:

  • Observation: Where can you see the enemy? Where can the enemy see you? Good observation enables effective fire and early warning. Poor observation creates surprise.

  • Cover and concealment: Cover protects from fire. Concealment hides from observation. The section commander must identify both and use them to protect the section.

  • Obstacles: Natural or artificial features that impede movement. Rivers, walls, minefields, wire. Obstacles can protect flanks or block routes of advance.

  • Key terrain: Any feature whose seizure, retention, or control provides a marked advantage to either side. A hilltop. A bridge. A road junction. Key terrain is the spatial focus of the battle.

  • Avenues of attack: Routes along which a force can move to reach its objective. The section commander must identify covered and concealed avenues that allow the section to close with the enemy.

docs.title: Ground and Movement
docs.text:
The section commander must calculate not merely the distance to an objective, but the time required to traverse that distance in the specific terrain. A kilometre of open ground takes minutes. A kilometre of dense vegetation takes longer. A kilometre under fire takes longest of all.

Ground also determines the formation the section adopts. Open terrain may allow a wide skirmish line. Jungle requires a single file. Urban terrain requires bounding overwatch between buildings.

docs.title: Fighting the Battle
docs.text: The section commander fights the battle through fire and movement. Fire suppresses the enemy. Movement closes the distance. The combination of fire and movement is the fundamental tactic of land warfare.

docs.title: Fire and Movement
docs.text: Fire and movement requires one element to suppress the enemy while another element moves. The section commander designates which fire team suppresses and which moves. The timing is critical. If the suppressing fire lifts too early, the moving team is exposed. If it lifts too late, the moving team cannot advance.

docs.title: Fire Control
docs.text: The section commander controls fire through fire orders. Fire orders include the target indication, the rate of fire, and the duration of fire. The section commander must ensure that all members of the section understand the fire orders and can deliver accurate fire on the target.

docs.title: Close Combat
docs.text:
The section commander must be prepared to close with the enemy. Close combat is the defining characteristic of land warfare. The section that closes with the enemy and destroys or captures them achieves the objective.

Close combat requires aggression, training, and unit cohesion. The section commander must inspire the section to fight at close quarters and overcome the natural resistance to killing.

docs.title: Holding the Ground
docs.text: Seizing ground is only half the battle. The section must hold the ground against counterattack. Holding requires preparation, organisation, and the will to defend.

docs.title: Hasty Defence
docs.text: When the section seizes an objective, it immediately organises a hasty defence. The section commander designates primary and alternate positions. Fields of fire are cleared. Ammunition is redistributed. The section prepares for the inevitable counterattack.

docs.title: Positions
docs.text: The section commander positions the section to maximise firepower while minimising exposure. Positions must provide cover from fire and observation. They must also provide fields of fire that cover the likely avenues of enemy approach.

docs.title: Sectors of Fire
docs.text: The section commander assigns sectors of fire to each fire team. Sectors of fire ensure that all approaches are covered. They also prevent fratricide by ensuring that each fire team knows where friendly forces are located.

docs.title: The Section Commander's Landward Problem
docs.text:
The section commander faces a unique problem in the landward domain. The section commander must simultaneously read the ground, fight the battle, and hold the ground. These tasks are interdependent. Reading the ground enables effective fighting. Fighting enables holding the ground. Holding the ground provides the platform for the next advance.

The section commander who masters this cycle is the section commander who wins.

docs.title: Maritime Domain — Nature and Military Relevance
docs.text:
"The United States is the most powerful nation on earth, dependent upon transoceanic links commercial and military to allies, friends, and interests." — Naval Doctrine Publication 1

The maritime domain is the vast expanse of water that covers approximately 71 percent of the Earth's surface. It includes the oceans, seas, estuaries, coastal waters, and the airspace above them. It is the medium through which 90 percent of global trade flows and the arena in which naval forces have contested for centuries.

This page examines the nature of the maritime domain, its enduring characteristics, and its centrality to military operations.

docs.title: The Nature of the Maritime Domain
A Global Commons
docs.text:
The maritime domain is the ultimate global commons. Unlike land territory, which is subject to national sovereignty, much of the ocean is international water. Ships of all nations traverse these waters in peace and war. This freedom of navigation is the foundation of global commerce and naval power projection.

The law of the sea, codified in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), establishes the legal framework for maritime operations. Coastal states exercise sovereignty over their territorial seas (up to 12 nautical miles) and jurisdiction over their exclusive economic zones (up to 200 nautical miles). Beyond these limits lie the high seas, open to all.

docs.title: A Three-Dimensional Battlespace
docs.text:
The maritime domain is unique in its three-dimensional character. Operations occur simultaneously in three dimensions:

  • Up: Air warfare and air defence above the fleet
  • Out: Surface warfare across the sea
  • Down: Undersea warfare beneath the surface

Each dimension presents distinct challenges. Aircraft operate at high speed but limited endurance. Surface ships provide persistent presence but are vulnerable to air and submarine attack. Submarines offer stealth and endurance but limited sensors and weapons.

docs.title: The Scouting Problem
docs.text:
The defining characteristic of naval combat is the vastness of the ocean and the difficulty of finding the enemy. Wayne Hughes, the dean of naval tacticians, wrote that "the battle will be decided by scouting effectiveness and weapon range" (Hughes, Fleet Tactics and Naval Operations, 2018).

In the age of sail, scouting was limited to the horizon. In the modern era, sensors extend far beyond the horizon, but so do weapons. The modern naval duel is a race between scouting and weapons. The force that finds the enemy first and strikes first generally wins.

docs.title: The Navy's Foremost Function: Sea Control
docs.text:
Sea control is the Navy's primary objective. Without sea control, no other naval function is possible. Sea control enables the movement of military and commercial shipping. It enables the projection of power ashore. It enables the blockade of an enemy's coast.

Sea control is geographic and time-based. No navy can control all the sea all the time. Sea control is established "for just long enough, over just enough area, to achieve a desired outcome" (JDP 0-10). It is a spectrum of activity, from local sea control in a confined waterway to oceanic command of the sea.

Sea denial is the opposite of sea control. Sea denial prevents an enemy from using the sea. It is achieved through submarines, mines, land-based anti-ship missiles, and asymmetric tactics.

docs.title: Enduring Characteristics of the Maritime Domain
1. The Primacy of Attrition
docs.text: Naval combat is fundamentally a process of attrition. Attrition comes from the successful delivery of firepower. The force that delivers more effective firepower over time prevails. This is true whether the combatants are galleys exchanging cannon broadsides or destroyers launching anti-ship missiles.

docs.title: 2. Scouting Determines Victory
docs.text: Scouting — locating the enemy sufficiently to deliver effective firepower — is the crucial process of naval tactics. The force that scouts more effectively gains the initiative and strikes first. Hughes wrote that "the choice of tactics will also be governed by scouting effectiveness and weapons range."

docs.title: 3. Command and Control Transforms Potential into Reality
docs.text: Command and control (C2) transforms scouting and firepower potential into the reality of delivered force. The force with better C2 — better situational awareness, better decision-making, better coordination — will prevail. In the age of network-centric warfare, C2 is both a strength and a vulnerability.

docs.title: 4. Maneuver Positions Forces to Scout and Shoot
docs.text: Maneuver is the activity by which C2 positions forces to scout and shoot. The force that maneuvers more effectively gains the advantage. Maneuver in the modern era is not merely geographic positioning. It is the integration of capabilities across domains — the orchestration of sensing, shooting, and countersensor/shooting capabilities across the entire fleet.

docs.title: 5. The Side That Attacks Effectively First Generally Wins
docs.text: Hughes's basic precept is that naval combat is a duel, and the side that attacks effectively first generally wins. This is the temporal equivalent of the land warfare principle of seizing the initiative. The force that acts inside the enemy's decision cycle gains a cumulative advantage.

docs.title: 6. Maritime Forces Are Self-Sustaining
docs.text: Maritime forces can deploy independently and provide a persistent, self-sustaining forward presence. Ships carry their own logistics — fuel, food, ammunition, and spare parts. This self-sustaining quality gives maritime forces unique strategic flexibility.

docs.title: 7. Maritime Power Enables Joint Operations
docs.text: Maritime power enables joint operations. Sea control enables the movement of land forces by sea. Aircraft carriers provide airpower independent of land bases. Amphibious forces project power from sea to land. The maritime domain is the enabling medium for joint campaigns.

docs.title: Naval Warfare Areas
docs.text: Naval forces fight in multiple warfare areas simultaneously:

docs.title: Surface Warfare
docs.text: Surface warfare is the massing of fires to take or sink enemy ships. It has evolved from cannon broadsides to a combined-arms effort involving aircraft, ships, submarines, and shore-based systems.

docs.title: Undersea Warfare
docs.text: Undersea warfare encompasses actions to establish and maintain control of the undersea portion of the maritime domain. It includes antisubmarine warfare, mine warfare, and submarine operations. Undersea warfare remains the most intricate and complex tactical problem.

docs.title: Air and Missile Defence
docs.text: Air and missile defence protects the fleet from aircraft, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles. It includes active and passive measures — fighters, surface-to-air missiles, electronic warfare, and decoys.

docs.title: Strike Warfare
docs.text: Strike warfare is the use of naval forces to deliver lethal and nonlethal fires to create desired effects against targets on land. It includes aircraft strikes, cruise missile strikes, and naval gunfire support.

docs.title: Amphibious Warfare
docs.text: Amphibious warfare is the projection of naval forces into, and their employment within or from, a foreign country and adjacent waters. It includes amphibious assaults, raids, and withdrawals.

docs.title: Mine Warfare
docs.text: Mine warfare includes the laying of mines to deny sea areas to the enemy and the clearing of mines to enable friendly operations. Mines are the most cost-effective sea denial weapon.

docs.title: Information Warfare
docs.text: Information warfare encompasses operations to exploit, deceive, degrade, or destroy enemy information and information systems. It includes electronic warfare, cyber operations, psychological operations, and deception.

docs.title: The Maritime Domain and Multi-Domain Operations
docs.text:
Modern maritime operations are inherently multi-domain. Maritime forces operate in the air, on the sea surface, under the sea, in space, and in cyberspace. They enable operations on land. They depend on space-based communications and positioning. They are vulnerable to cyber attack.

The future of maritime operations lies in distributed lethality — the integration of capabilities across widely distributed platforms. This requires tight integration of sensing, shooting, and C2 across the fleet, loosening the ties of geography and organisational boundaries.

docs.title: Implications for Military Operations
docs.text:
The maritime domain has direct implications at every level of war:

  • Strategic: Maritime power enables global power projection. Control of the seas enables the movement of military and commercial shipping. Denial of the seas can strangle an enemy's economy.

  • Operational: Maritime campaigns are designed to achieve sea control and project power ashore. The arrangement of naval forces to support joint campaigns is the essence of operational art at sea.

  • Tactical: Naval engagements are fought at specific locations and times. The coordination of surface, air, and undersea forces to destroy enemy naval forces is the essence of naval tactics.

docs.title: Case Study — Falklands War (1982): Maritime Power in a Littoral Campaign
docs.text:
"The British victory would have to be judged anyway as a fairly close run thing... We fought our way along a knife-edge." — Admiral Sir John Woodward, Task Force Commander

This case study examines the 1982 Falkland Islands campaign, the largest maritime campaign since the Second World War. It demonstrates the application of maritime power to achieve political objectives in a littoral environment.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: On 2 April 1982, Argentine forces invaded and occupied the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas), a British overseas territory 275 nautical miles from Argentina and 6,700 nautical miles from Britain. The British government resolved to retake the islands by force. The campaign lasted 74 days.

docs.title: British Challenges
docs.text:
Britain faced a severe logistical challenge. The nearest British base was Ascension Island, 3,500 nautical miles from the Falklands. The task force would have to operate 8,000 miles from home with no local infrastructure.

Britain had only two small aircraft carriers (HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible), 33 Sea Harrier V/STOL fighters, and a limited number of escorts. There was no airborne early warning (AEW) capability. The Royal Navy had been cut back in recent years and was not designed for this type of operation.

docs.title: Argentine Advantages
docs.text: Argentina enjoyed significant geographic advantage. The Falklands were within range of Argentine land-based aircraft. Argentina possessed a fleet of 17 combatant ships, three submarines, and approximately 130 operational fixed-wing attack aircraft, including Dassault Super Etendards armed with Exocet anti-ship missiles.

docs.title: Deployment (April 1982)
docs.text: The British task force sailed from Britain on 5 April. Rear Admiral John Woodward's carrier battle group departed Ascension Island on 18 April, arriving in the Total Exclusion Zone around the Falklands on 1 May.

docs.title: Sea Control (May 1982)
docs.text:
The first priority was sea control. On 2 May, the nuclear submarine HMS Conqueror sank the Argentine cruiser ARA General Belgrano with two torpedo hits. The Argentine Navy, fearful of further submarine attacks, withdrew its surface fleet to port for the remainder of the war.

This single action eliminated the Argentine surface navy from the campaign. It was a decisive application of undersea warfare.

docs.title: Air Superiority (May 1982)
docs.text:
The Sea Harriers flew combat air patrols over the task force and strike missions against Argentine positions. They proved highly effective, shooting down 20 Argentine aircraft without loss in air-to-air combat.

However, the British lacked AEW. Argentine aircraft could approach at low level and attack before being detected. The task force suffered losses. HMS Sheffield was sunk by an Exocet missile on 4 May. HMS Coventry was sunk by bombs on 25 May. Three other ships were damaged.

docs.title: The Amphibious Landing
docs.text:
On 21 May, the amphibious task force landed 3 Commando Brigade at San Carlos Water on East Falkland. The landing was unopposed, but Argentine aircraft attacked the ships in the anchorage.

The British established a beachhead at San Carlos and began the advance toward Port Stanley. The land campaign lasted three weeks. Port Stanley fell on 14 June, and the Argentine garrison surrendered.

docs.title: 1. Sea Control Is Essential
docs.text: British success depended on establishing sea control. Without sea control, the amphibious landing would have been impossible. The sinking of the Belgrano was the decisive action that secured sea control.

docs.title: 2. Submarines Are Decisive
docs.text: The single submarine HMS Conqueror eliminated an entire navy. The undersea domain is the most asymmetric domain. A small submarine force can achieve disproportionate effects.

docs.title: 3. AEW Is Essential
docs.text: The lack of AEW was the most significant British deficiency. Argentine aircraft could approach at low level and attack before being detected. AEW would have extended the detection range and increased the effectiveness of the Sea Harriers.

docs.title: 4. The Sea Harrier Was Decisive
docs.text: The Sea Harrier proved that a small number of highly capable aircraft can achieve air superiority. The Sea Harrier shot down 20 Argentine aircraft without loss. It demonstrated the value of V/STOL aircraft in maritime operations.

docs.title: 5. Integrated Defence Is Required
docs.text: The San Carlos anchorage was defended by an integrated system: Sea Harriers patrolled the airspace, surface ships provided missile defence, and ground forces provided close-in defence. This integrated defence defeated the Argentine air attacks.

docs.title: 6. Logistics Determine the Campaign
docs.text: The campaign was a logistical feat. The task force operated 8,000 miles from home. Merchant ships were requisitioned to carry supplies and troops. The campaign demonstrated the importance of logistics in maritime operations.

docs.title: 7. The Littoral Is the Future
docs.text: The Falklands campaign was a littoral campaign. The maritime, land, and air domains were closely integrated. The littoral is the most complex operational environment. Future campaigns will be fought in the littorals.

docs.title: Ship Captain's Maritime Operations — Commanding the Vessel in the Maritime Domain
docs.text:
"The captain of a warship is the direct representative of the state. The captain's authority is absolute aboard the vessel." — NWP 1-14M, The Commander's Handbook on the Law of Naval Operations

The ship captain operates at the most granular level of maritime command. The captain is responsible for the safety of the ship, the crew, and the mission. In combat, the captain must make decisions in seconds, often without consulting higher authority.

This page discusses the maritime domain at the ship level, relevant to commanding officers of warships from patrol vessels to aircraft carriers.

docs.title: The Captain's Maritime Environment
docs.text: The captain operates in a three-dimensional battlespace. Threats can come from above (aircraft, missiles), from the surface (enemy ships), and from below (submarines, mines). The captain must maintain awareness in all three dimensions simultaneously.

docs.title: The OODA Loop at Sea
docs.text:
Boyd's OODA loop applies at the ship level. The captain who observes the threat first, orients correctly, decides quickly, and acts decisively gains the advantage. In a missile duel, the cycle can compress to seconds.

The captain must balance the need for emission control (avoiding detection) against the need for situational awareness (detecting the enemy). Emitting radar signals reveals the ship's position. Remaining passive risks being surprised. This is the fundamental tension of modern naval operations.

docs.title: Scouting
docs.text:
The captain must find the enemy before the enemy finds the ship. Scouting is the most critical process in naval combat. The captain uses organic sensors (radar, sonar, electronic warfare) and off-ship information (satellite, aircraft, other ships) to build a picture of the battlespace.

In a distributed lethality concept, each ship must be capable of independent scouting. The captain cannot rely solely on off-ship sensors. Organic sensors — shipborne radar, sonar, and electronic warfare systems — are the ship's primary means of finding the enemy.

docs.title: Weapons Employment
docs.text:
The captain employs weapons based on the tactical situation. Anti-ship missiles are the primary weapon for surface warfare. Surface-to-air missiles defend against air threats. Torpedoes and depth charges engage submarines. The captain must decide when to employ weapons and which weapons to use.

The decision to employ weapons is a command decision. The captain must weigh the risk of revealing the ship's position against the need to destroy the enemy. In emission control conditions, the captain may choose to remain passive until the enemy is within weapons range.

docs.title: Manoeuvre
docs.text: The captain manoeuvres the ship to gain tactical advantage. Manoeuvre positions the ship for scouting and shooting. It also reduces the ship's vulnerability to enemy weapons. Evasive manoeuvring can defeat incoming missiles. High speed reduces the submarine threat.

docs.title: Surface Warfare
docs.text: The captain fights surface actions using anti-ship missiles, guns, and electronic warfare. The modern surface action is a missile duel. The ship that launches first and scores hits generally wins.

docs.title: Anti-Air Warfare
docs.text: The captain defends the ship against aircraft and missile attacks. Air defence is layered: outer layer (fighters), middle layer (surface-to-air missiles), inner layer (close-in weapons systems). The captain must coordinate these layers and decide when to engage.

docs.title: Anti-Submarine Warfare
docs.text: The captain fights submarines using sonar, torpedoes, and depth charges. Submarines are the most difficult threat to detect and engage. The captain must maintain constant vigilance against submarine attack.

docs.title: Mine Warfare
docs.text: The captain avoids mines using mine-hunting sonar and route planning. Mines are the most cost-effective sea denial weapon. A single mine can disable or sink a warship.

docs.title: The Captain's Legal Obligations
docs.text:
The captain has legal obligations under the law of the sea and the law of armed conflict. The captain must respect the sovereignty of coastal states in their territorial seas. The captain must comply with the rules of engagement. The captain must treat prisoners humanely and respect the rights of neutral vessels.

These legal obligations are not constraints on operations. They are the framework within which legitimate military operations are conducted.

docs.title: The Captain's Landward Problem
docs.text:
The captain faces a unique problem in the maritime domain. The captain must simultaneously scout for the enemy, employ weapons, manoeuvre the ship, and comply with legal obligations. These tasks are interdependent. Scouting enables effective weapons employment. Weapons employment enables manoeuvre. Manoeuvre enables continued scouting.

The captain who masters this cycle is the captain who brings the ship and crew home.

docs.title: Task Group Commander's Maritime Operations — Leading the Surface Action Group
docs.text:
"The essence of distributed lethality is that continuous emissions will be fatal and allow the enemy to strike first." — CAPT (Ret.) Wayne P. Hughes Jr.

The task group commander leads a Surface Action Group (SAG) or similar formation. The task group is the basic tactical formation of the surface navy. It consists of multiple ships operating together under a single commander. The task group commander must coordinate the actions of multiple ships while empowering individual captains to act independently.

This page discusses the maritime domain at the task group level, relevant to commanders of destroyer squadrons, amphibious ready groups, and similar formations.

docs.title: The Task Group Commander's Maritime Problem
docs.text: The task group commander operates in a three-dimensional battlespace. The commander must coordinate anti-surface, anti-air, and anti-submarine warfare simultaneously. The commander must balance the need for concentrated firepower against the risk of concentrated enemy attack.

docs.title: The Distributed Lethality Concept
docs.text:
Modern naval operations emphasise distributed lethality. Rather than concentrating all ships in a tight formation, distributed lethality spreads ships across a wide area. Each ship operates as an independent kill platform. The group achieves cumulative sea control through distributed operations.

The task group commander must trust individual captains to act on commander's intent without waiting for orders. This requires mission command — the delegation of authority to the lowest level of command.

docs.title: The Scouting Problem
docs.text:
The task group commander must maintain a comprehensive picture of the battlespace. This requires integrating information from multiple sources: ship sensors, aircraft, submarines, satellites, and other forces. The commander must process this information quickly and make decisions in seconds.

In emission control conditions, the task group may have to operate passively. The commander must weigh the need for information against the risk of detection.

docs.title: The Task Group Commander's Tactical Decisions
Formation
docs.text:
The task group commander selects the formation based on the threat. For air defence, circular formations provide the best protection. For surface warfare, formations with width provide better scouting. For submarine warfare, formations with depth are preferred.

The task group commander must be able to shift formations quickly as the threat changes. The transition from one formation to another is a vulnerable moment.

docs.title: Weapons Employment
docs.text: The task group commander coordinates weapons employment across multiple ships. The commander must prevent fratire and ensure that weapons are used effectively. The commander must decide when to employ long-range weapons and when to conserve them for close-range engagement.

docs.title: Manoeuvre
docs.text: The task group commander manoeuvres the group to gain tactical advantage. Manoeuvre positions the group for scouting and shooting. It also reduces the group's vulnerability to enemy weapons. The task group commander must coordinate the movement of multiple ships while maintaining formation integrity.

docs.title: The Task Group Commander's Warfare Areas
Anti-Surface Warfare
docs.text: The task group commander fights surface actions using coordinated anti-ship missile attacks. The goal is to destroy the enemy's surface combatants before they can launch their own missiles. The task group commander must coordinate the timing of missile launches to achieve maximum effect.

docs.title: Anti-Air Warfare
docs.text: The task group commander defends the group against air attack. Air defence is coordinated across multiple ships. The task group commander assigns sectors of responsibility to individual ships and coordinates the employment of surface-to-air missiles.

docs.title: Anti-Submarine Warfare
docs.text: The task group commander coordinates anti-submarine operations across the group. The commander assigns anti-submarine helicopters to search sectors and coordinates the employment of torpedoes and depth charges.

docs.title: Amphibious Operations
docs.text: The task group commander supports amphibious operations by providing fire support, air defence, and sea control. The commander must coordinate the movement of amphibious shipping and protect it from enemy attack.

docs.title: The Task Group Commander and Mission Command
docs.text:
The task group commander practises mission command. The commander provides intent and guidance but trusts individual captains to execute. This requires mutual trust and shared understanding. It also requires captains who are trained to act independently.

Mission command in the maritime domain is complicated by the vastness of the ocean and the difficulty of communication. The task group commander must be prepared to operate in emission control conditions where communication is limited or impossible.

docs.title: The Task Group Commander's Landward Problem
docs.text:
The task group commander faces a complex maritime problem. The commander must simultaneously coordinate multiple ships, maintain situational awareness in three dimensions, and respond to threats from the air, surface, and subsurface. The commander must balance the need for concentrated firepower against the risk of concentrated attack.

The task group commander who masters distributed lethality and mission command is the task group commander who wins.

docs.title: Battalion Staff Sensemaking — The Cognitive Architecture of Command
docs.text: "The battle staff is that element within the organisation which helps the commander create and refine the battlefield image." — Kahan, Battle Staff Integration, 1994

docs.title: Organisational Cognition at Battalion Level
docs.text:
A major serves as a company commander or battalion staff officer. At this level, individual sensemaking is necessary but not sufficient. The battalion must make sense of the battlefield as an organisation. The staff processes information from multiple companies. The commander blends that information with experience and judgement. Together, they form a shared picture that no single person could build alone.

This page covers the noetic work of battalion command. It focuses on how a staff builds and maintains a shared understanding of the battlefield, and how a major contributes to that process.

docs.title: Battle Tracking
docs.text:
Battle tracking is the process of developing and refining a shared image of the battlefield. The staff collects, processes, analyses, and monitors information. The commander uses that image to make decisions and focus combat power. Effective battle tracking requires:

  • Information sharing across functions. Intelligence, operations, and logistics must share what they know. Stove-pipes kill shared understanding.
  • A common reference point. The common operational picture (COP) gives everyone the same frame of reference.
  • Mutual awareness. Each staff officer must understand what the others need to know.

docs.title: The Battle Rhythm
docs.text:
The battle rhythm synchronises staff activities. It sets a cycle of meetings, briefings, and updates. The standard rhythm includes:

  • Commander's update briefing. The S2 and S3 brief the current situation.
  • Operations update. Subordinate units report their status.
  • Plans meeting. The staff develops or refines courses of action.
  • Targeting meeting. The fire support team synchronises fires.

But rigid battle rhythms can fail. When operations accelerate, meetings become impossible. The staff must adapt. A flexible battle rhythm compresses or expands as the fight demands. The commander and staff must maintain shared understanding through running estimates and informal processes when formal meetings are not possible.

docs.title: Intelligence and Operations as a Cognitive Partnership
docs.text:
The S2 (intelligence officer) and S3 (operations officer) must work as a team. The S2 focuses on the enemy. The S3 focuses on friendly operations. Neither can succeed alone.

The S2's cognitive work: - Conducts intelligence preparation of the battlefield (IPB). - Develops enemy courses of action and situation templates. - Identifies high-value targets and named areas of interest. - Answers the commander's priority intelligence requirements.

The S3's cognitive work: - Develops friendly courses of action. - Synchronises the operations order. - Coordinates fire support, engineer assets, and manoeuvre. - Tracks the execution of operations.

Together, they wargame friendly plans against enemy plans. They identify decision points. They build the synchronisation matrix.

docs.title: The S2 Must Drive Scout Planning
docs.text: The S2 must give the scout platoon precise guidance. The scout platoon leader needs to know what to look for, where to look, and when to report. The S2 develops the reconnaissance and surveillance (R&S) plan. The S3 translates that plan into operational terms.

docs.title: What the Commander Needs to Know
docs.text:
The commander sets the CCIR — the information needed to make decisions. The staff must understand what the commander needs and why. The CCIR drives the collection plan. It focuses scarce reconnaissance assets on the most important questions.

Common CCIR at battalion level include: - Will the enemy counterattack? - Where is the enemy main effort? - What is the status of the adjacent unit's sector? - Are the bridges on the main supply route intact?

The staff must anticipate the commander's information needs. Good staff officers think ahead. They provide the commander with the information needed for the next decision, not just the current one.

docs.title: Building the COP
docs.text:
The COP is the shared visual display of the battlefield. It shows friendly positions, enemy positions, and control measures. The S2 builds the enemy picture. The S3 builds the friendly picture. Together they create the fused COP.

At battalion level, the COP comes from many sources: - Spot reports from subordinate units. - Sensor feeds (UAV, radar, signals intelligence). - Reports from adjacent units. - Intelligence reach from higher headquarters.

The S2 fuses these inputs. The result is a picture that is never complete. The S2 must confirm or deny enemy courses of action. They must fill gaps in knowledge.

docs.title: The Limits of the COP
docs.text:
The COP is a model, not reality. It is always incomplete. Sometimes it is wrong. The staff must understand its limits:

  • Friendly reports are more reliable than enemy reports. Friendly units know their own positions. Enemy positions are estimates.
  • The enemy COP is the hardest to build. Enemy icons on the COP represent the best available assessment, not confirmed fact.
  • Redundancy must be removed. Multiple observers may report the same enemy unit. The S2 must eliminate duplicate icons.

docs.title: As Company Commander
docs.text:
As a company commander, you are the primary sensemaker for your company. You receive the battalion commander's intent. You develop your company concept. You coordinate with adjacent companies. You maintain awareness of the battalion situation one level higher.

Your cognitive work includes: - Understanding the battalion end state. What must the battalion achieve? - Translating intent into company orders. What must your company do? - Maintaining situational awareness. What is happening in adjacent sectors? - Making decisions in contact. When the plan changes, you must adapt.

docs.title: As Battalion Staff Officer
docs.text:
As a staff officer (S2 or S3), you support the battalion commander's sensemaking. You process information. You develop products. You anticipate needs. You coordinate with the adjacent staff sections.

Your cognitive work includes: - Running estimates. You maintain a continuous estimate of the situation in your functional area. - Briefing the commander. You distil complex information into clear assessments. - Coordinating with peers. You share information with the other staff sections. - Driving the collection plan. You task reconnaissance assets to answer the commander's questions.

docs.title: The Battalion as a Cognitive Network
docs.text:
The battalion is a network of sensemakers. Each company commander interprets the situation in their sector. Each staff officer interprets it through their functional lens. The commander fuses these interpretations into a coherent picture.

Research on distributed sensemaking identifies nine principles for supporting it in military teams. The most important for battalion staff are:

  1. Represent information quality and provenance. Show what is known, what is suspected, and what is templated.
  2. Promote expertise. Each staff officer must be the expert in their area.
  3. Minimise the cost of achieving common ground. Make it easy for staff to share information and reach shared understanding.
  4. Provide explanatory context. Do not just report facts. Explain what they mean.

docs.title: Staff Exercises
docs.text: Train the staff through realistic exercises. Use scenarios that require information sharing, assessment, and decision-making. Debrief the process, not only the product. Ask: What did the staff miss? Why? How can we improve?

docs.title: Build Intelligence Literacy
docs.text: At battalion level, the staff is small enough to train for intelligence literacy. Every staff officer should understand the IPB process, the collection plan, and the intelligence estimate. The S2 cannot do everything alone. The whole staff must think about the enemy.
