docs.title: The Platoon Commander's Cognitive Domain — Translating Intent into Action
docs.text: "The platoon leader must have a relatively complete knowledge of the terrain, and he must know as much as possible about the enemy." — FM 17-98, Scout Platoon, U.S. Department of the Army

docs.title: The Cognitive Leap to Platoon Command
docs.text:
A lieutenant commands a platoon of 30 soldiers. The cognitive demand jumps sharply from section command. You now coordinate multiple sections. You maintain situational awareness across a larger area. You translate company commander's intent into platoon orders. You make decisions in contact when information is contradictory and time is short.

This page covers the noetic work of platoon command. It focuses on the cognitive demands that distinguish a lieutenant from a corporal.

docs.title: Three Levels of Awareness
docs.text:
Endsley's model defines three levels of situation awareness:

  1. Level 1 — Perception. You see the relevant elements in the environment. At platoon level, this means knowing where your sections are, where the enemy is, and what the terrain looks like.

  2. Level 2 — Comprehension. You understand what those elements mean. You recognise that the enemy is forming up for an attack, not just moving. You understand that a terrain feature blocks your fields of fire.

  3. Level 3 — Projection. You predict what will happen next. You anticipate where the enemy will move. You foresee how the terrain will affect the battle in the next 30 minutes.

Research with infantry platoon leaders shows that experienced officers attend more to enemy locations and strengths. Less experienced officers attend more to friendly strengths. Train yourself to focus on the enemy and the terrain.

docs.title: Maintaining Awareness Across the Platoon
docs.text:
Your platoon operates dispersed. Each section sees a different piece of the battlefield. Your job is to build a coherent picture from these fragments. To do this:

  • Establish a reporting rhythm. Tell sections when to report. Enforce it.
  • Use a map. Plot friendly positions one level higher. Plot enemy spot reports as they come in.
  • Ask the right questions. When a section reports, ask: What do you see? What do you hear? What do you think it means?

docs.title: The Burden of Command
docs.text:
Research shows that platoon leaders face high cognitive workload. You monitor the tactical display. You listen to the radio. You observe the battlefield. You issue orders. You coordinate with adjacent platoons. All at once.

Studies on message presentation rate show that fast rates increase cognitive load and degrade situation awareness. Visual messages (text) create higher load than auditory ones (radio voice). When information comes too fast, you lose awareness and make worse decisions.

docs.title: Managing Your Load
docs.text:
To manage cognitive load:

  • Prioritise. Not every piece of information needs your immediate attention. Filter.
  • Delegate. Trust your platoon sergeant to handle administration and logistics. Focus on the fight.
  • Use your map. Offload memory to the map. Plot positions instead of holding them in your head.
  • Pause when you can. Even a 10-second pause helps you reassess.

docs.title: Understanding the Company Commander's Intent
docs.text:
The company commander's intent tells you what the company must achieve and why. Your job is to translate that intent into a platoon concept. You must understand:

  • The company end state. What does success look like for the company?
  • The platoon task. What must your platoon do to support the company?
  • The key tasks. What must be achieved regardless of course of action?

docs.title: Giving Clear Orders
docs.text:
Your platoon order must be clear enough for section commanders to act when they cannot reach you. Use the standard format (SMEAC: Situation, Mission, Execution, Administration, Command). Keep it simple. Tell section commanders:

  • What the platoon will do.
  • What their section will do.
  • Why it matters.
  • What to do if the plan changes.

docs.title: Distributed Cognition
docs.text:
You and your platoon sergeant form a two-person command team. This is a distributed cognitive system. You focus on the enemy and the battle. He focuses on the platoon's readiness, ammunition, casualties, and logistics. Together, you maintain a more complete picture than either could alone.

To make this work:

  • Trust him. Give him authority over administrative and logistical matters.
  • Communicate constantly. Share what you see and what you think. Ask for his assessment.
  • Back him up. When he makes a decision within his authority, support it.

docs.title: The OODA Loop Under Fire
docs.text:
In contact, your OODA loop compresses. You observe the enemy. You orient using your understanding of the terrain and the enemy. You decide on a course of action. You act. Then you start again.

Under stress, the loop can break. You may fixate on one piece of information. You may fail to update your assessment. To prevent this:

  • Keep asking questions. What has changed? What am I missing?
  • Use your platoon sergeant. He sees things you do not.
  • Accept risk. You will never have perfect information. Decide with what you have.

docs.title: Recognition-Primed Decisions
docs.text:
Klein's research shows that experienced leaders recognise situations and respond almost automatically. They do not compare options. They recognise the pattern. They mentally simulate a response. If it works, they act.

To build this skill:

  • Study past battles. Learn the patterns of tactical situations.
  • Do tactical decision games. Practise recognising situations and choosing responses.
  • Reflect after every exercise. What did you miss? What would you do differently?

docs.title: Training Your Platoon's Sensemaking
docs.text:
Your section commanders are sensemakers too. Train them:

  • Give them the intent. Always explain why, not just what.
  • Use rehearsals. Rehearsals build shared understanding. Every section commander should know what the others will do.
  • Debrief honestly. After every exercise, discuss what was missed and why.

docs.title: Section Commander's Sensemaking — Reading Ground, Enemy, and Intent
docs.text: "Sensemaking is the process by which people interpret ambiguous situations and decide how to act." — Weick, Sensemaking in Organizations, 1995

docs.title: The Cognitive Work of the Junior Leader
docs.text:
A section commander (lance corporal or corporal) operates at the lowest tactical level. Your cognitive work is immediate: read the ground, read the enemy, understand your commander's intent, and act. You do not have time for extended analysis. You must recognise patterns quickly and decide under stress.

This page covers the noetic demands of junior leadership. It focuses on practical sensemaking — what to look for, what to ignore, and how to communicate clearly when contact starts.

docs.title: OCOKA
docs.text:
Use the five factors of OCOKA to analyse terrain quickly:

  1. Observation and fields of fire. Where can you see the enemy? Where can the enemy see you? Identify positions that give your section good observation without exposing you to enemy fire.

  2. Cover and concealment. Cover protects you from fire. Concealment hides you from observation. A position can have concealment without cover (behind a bush in the open) or cover without concealment (a low wall the enemy can see over). Find positions with both.

  3. Obstacles. Natural or man-made features that stop, slow, or channel movement. Obstacles can befriend you if they block enemy approaches. They can hurt you if they trap your section in a kill zone.

  4. Key terrain. Any feature that gives a marked advantage to whoever controls it. At section level, key terrain may be a small rise, a crossing point, or a building that dominates the area.

  5. Avenues of approach. Routes along which an enemy force can move. Identify the most likely and most dangerous avenues. Position your section to cover them.

docs.title: Terrain Association
docs.text: Use terrain association to navigate and to maintain situational awareness. Match the contour intervals on your map to the features on the ground. Identify ridgelines, valleys, and man-made structures along your route. Update your position mentally as you move. Do not rely only on a GPS.

docs.title: Pattern Recognition
docs.text:
Enemy forces follow patterns. They use standard formations, timing, and tactics. Learn the patterns for the threat you face. Look for:

  • Signs of presence. Tracks, disturbed vegetation, fresh digging, smoke, or noise.
  • ** Likely positions.** The enemy will use the same logic you do. They want cover, concealment, good observation, and fields of fire. If you identify the best positions on the ground, the enemy probably has too.
  • Indicators of intent. Movement in a particular direction, digging in, or reconnaissance activity can reveal what the enemy plans to do.

docs.title: Recognition-Primed Decision Making
docs.text:
Klein's research shows that experienced leaders do not compare many options. They recognise the situation as similar to one they have seen before. They mentally simulate a course of action. If it works, they act. If not, they adjust.

At section level, this means:

  • Identify the type of situation. Is this an ambush? A hasty defence? A meeting engagement?
  • Mentally rehearse your response. Before you move, imagine what will happen. Check for obvious flaws.
  • Act decisively. Once you decide, move. Delay kills.

docs.title: Commander's Intent
docs.text:
Your platoon commander's intent tells you what the platoon must do and why. Your job is to understand it well enough to act when the plan changes. In contact, you may not receive orders. You must know what the commander wants to achieve. Then you can make the right decision.

At section level, understand:

  • The section's task. What must your section do?
  • The purpose. Why must you do it?
  • The commander's desired end state. What does success look like?

docs.title: Sense-Giving
docs.text: You are not only a sensemaker. You are also a sense-giver. You must communicate your understanding to your section. Tell them what you see, what you think it means, and what you want them to do. Clear, calm communication under fire is a cognitive skill. It requires practice.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
When you report to your platoon commander, follow a simple format:

  1. What you see. Describe the enemy or terrain feature.
  2. Where it is. Give a grid reference or a clear description.
  3. What you think it means. Give your assessment.
  4. What you plan to do. State your intended action.

Keep reports short. Use correct terminology. Do not guess. If you do not know something, say so.

docs.title: Managing Cognitive Load
docs.text:
Under stress, your working memory shrinks. You can hold fewer ideas at once. To manage this:

  • Use checklists. Memorise the key checks for your section (ammunition, casualties, position, enemy).
  • Chunk information. Group related facts together. Instead of reporting three separate enemy positions, report one enemy section in a specific area.
  • Breathe. Controlled breathing reduces stress and restores cognitive function.

docs.title: Training Your Sensemaking
docs.text:
Sensemaking is a trainable skill. To improve:

  • Practice terrain analysis. On every patrol or exercise, analyse the ground using OCOKA. Do it until it becomes automatic.
  • Study enemy tactics. Learn how the enemy fights. The more patterns you know, the faster you will recognise them.
  • Do decision exercises. Use tactical decision games (TDGs) to practise recognising situations and choosing responses.
  • Get feedback. After every exercise, ask your platoon commander or section members what you missed. Learn from it.

docs.title: Space-Time Domain — Nature and Military Relevance
docs.text:
"Space and time can no longer be thought of as an inert backdrop on which the events of the universe play themselves out; rather, through special and then general relativity, they are intimate players in the events themselves." — Frans Osinga, Science, Strategy and War

The space-time domain is not a physical domain like land, sea, or air. It is the dimension within which all military operations unfold. Space provides the geographic context — terrain, distance, elevation, weather. Time provides the temporal context — tempo, duration, sequence, synchronisation. Together, they form the framework within which commanders plan, decide, and act.

This domain is universal. Every operation, from a infantry section patrol to a multi-national campaign, exists within it. Mastery of the space-time domain is therefore not optional. It is foundational to all military art and science.

docs.title: The Nature of the Space-Time Domain
Space as a Military Factor
docs.text:
Space, in the military sense, refers to the physical environment in which forces operate. This includes terrain, vegetation, hydrography, climate, and human geography. Space determines where forces can move, where they can fight, and where they can hide.

Clausewitz treated space as one of the three elements of the "remarkable trinity" of war, alongside chance and probability (the primordial violence, enmity, and hatred) and policy (the subordination of war to reason). Space was, for Clausewitz, the canvas upon which the drama of war was painted.

Modern doctrine extends this. Space is not merely a passive container. It shapes the tempo of operations, the density of forces, the feasibility of manoeuvre, and the effectiveness of fires. Urban terrain compresses time and space. Open terrain expands them. Mountains channel movement. Rivers create obstacles.

docs.title: Time as a Military Factor
docs.text:
Time is the most constrained resource in war. Unlike ammunition or fuel, time cannot be stockpiled. Once lost, it cannot be recovered. Every military theorist from Sun Tzu to Clausewitz to Boyd has emphasised the centrality of time.

Sun Tzu wrote: "Speed is the essence of war. Take advantage of the enemy's unpreparedness; travel by unexpected routes and strike him where he has taken no precautions."

Clausewitz argued that time and space are the two media in which military force operates. He wrote that the concentration of forces in space and the unification of forces in time are the two great objects of military strategy.

Boyd went further. He argued that war is fundamentally a competition between opposing decision cycles, and that the ability to operate inside an adversary's decision cycle — to compress one's own time while stretching the enemy's — is the path to victory. This is the OODA loop: Observe, Orient, Decide, Act.

docs.title: The Fusion: Space-Time
docs.text:
Einstein's theory of relativity fused space and time into a single continuum. Military theorists have adopted this insight. Operations cannot be planned in space without reference to time, nor in time without reference to space.

A brigade attack is not merely a spatial event (the seizure of an objective). It is a temporal event (the synchronisation of multiple battalions at a specific time). A delay of minutes can mean the difference between success and failure. A miscalculation of terrain can render a perfectly timed plan irrelevant.

The space-time domain is therefore the integration of these two factors into a single operational framework.

docs.title: Enduring Characteristics of the Space-Time Domain
1. Time Is the One Irreversible Resource
docs.text:
All other military resources — personnel, equipment, ammunition, fuel — can be replaced or replenished. Time cannot. Every hour spent planning is an hour not spent executing. Every minute of delay is a minute the enemy uses to prepare.

This characteristic imposes a fundamental tension on all military decision-making: the tension between the desire for more information (which requires time) and the need to act quickly (which requires decisions with incomplete information).

docs.title: 2. Space Shapes Tempo
docs.text:
The physical environment directly affects the speed at which operations can be conducted. A mechanised force moves faster on open plains than in dense jungle. Infantry moves faster on roads than through mountains. Urban terrain slows all forces but particularly degrades technological advantages.

Commanders must therefore calculate not merely the spatial distance to an objective, but the temporal cost of traversing that distance in the specific terrain and conditions they face.

docs.title: 3. Tempo Is Relative, Not Absolute
docs.text:
Tempo is not raw speed. It is the rate of military activity relative to the adversary's rate. A force that moves slowly but disrupts the enemy's decision cycle more effectively than the enemy can respond has achieved tempo advantage.

This is Boyd's central insight. The goal is not to move as fast as possible, but to move faster than the enemy can comprehend and react to. Tempo is therefore a cognitive phenomenon as much as a physical one.

docs.title: 4. Synchronisation Requires Temporal Precision
docs.text:
Modern military operations involve the coordination of multiple units, formations, and capabilities across space and time. Synchronisation — the arrangement of actions in time and space to produce maximum combined effect — is a core requirement.

Synchronisation demands precise timing. Artillery must lift at the exact moment infantry advance. Air support must arrive at the specified time. Reserves must be committed at the decisive moment. Failure in any one temporal element can cascade into failure across the operation.

docs.title: 5. The Decision Cycle Is the Fundamental Unit of Tempo
docs.text:
Boyd's OODA loop is not merely a decision-making tool. It is a model of how organisations compete in time. The force that can observe, orient, decide, and act more quickly and effectively than its adversary gains a cumulative advantage.

Each cycle that completes inside the adversary's cycle creates confusion, disorder, and eventually paralysis in the enemy's decision-making. This is what Boyd meant by "getting inside the opponent's OODA loop."

docs.title: 6. Friction Degrades Both Space and Time
docs.text:
Clausewitz's concept of friction — the accumulation of small difficulties, errors, and uncertainties that make war difficult — applies directly to the space-time domain. Friction slows movement, disrupts synchronisation, and degrades decision-making.

A unit that planned to reach an objective in two hours may take four due to unexpected terrain, enemy contact, or equipment failure. A headquarters that planned to issue orders in thirty minutes may take ninety due to communication breakdowns. Friction is inevitable; managing it is the art of command.

docs.title: 7. Technology Compresses Space and Time
docs.text:
Advances in transportation, communication, and information technology have progressively compressed the space-time domain. Forces can move faster, communicate instantaneously across greater distances, and process information more quickly.

This compression has accelerated the tempo of operations. What required weeks in the Napoleonic era required days in the Second World War and hours in the Gulf War. The proliferation of precision-guided munitions, satellite communications, and real-time intelligence has further compressed the decision cycle.

docs.title: 8. The Space-Time Domain Is Contested
docs.text:
Adversaries actively seek to disrupt friendly operations in the space-time domain. They mine terrain to slow movement. They jam communications to disrupt synchronisation. They conduct deception to distort the enemy's orientation. They strike headquarters to paralyse decision-making.

Countering these threats requires active measures: route clearance, electronic warfare, counter-deception, and mission command that enables subordinate commanders to act when higher headquarters are disrupted.

docs.title: Implications for Military Operations
docs.text:
The space-time domain has direct implications at every level of war:

  • Strategic: Campaigns are planned across vast distances and extended timeframes. The concentration of forces in space and time — the assembly of overwhelming combat power at the decisive point — is the essence of strategy.

  • Operational: The arrangement of battles and major operations in space and time to achieve strategic objectives. The sequencing of offensives, the allocation of reserves, and the synchronisation of joint and multinational forces are all space-time problems.

  • Tactical: The execution of battles and engagements at specific locations and times. The coordination of infantry, armour, artillery, and air support in the attack or defence is fundamentally a space-time challenge.

docs.title: Battalion Staff Space-Time — The Cognitive Architecture of Command
docs.text:
"The battle staff is that element within the organisation which helps the commander create and refine the battlefield image." — FM 6-0, Commander and Staff Organization and Operations

The battalion commander operates at the tactical level where multiple companies are coordinated in space and time. The battalion staff — S1 (personnel), S2 (intelligence), S3 (operations), S4 (logistics), and supporting cells — enables the commander to visualise the battlespace, make decisions, and synchronise the actions of subordinate units.

This page discusses the space-time domain at the battalion staff level, relevant to majors, captains, and staff officers.

docs.title: The Battalion Staff's Spatial Problem
docs.text: The battalion staff must maintain a common operating picture (COP) of the battlespace. This requires the integration of information from multiple sources: company reports, intelligence feeds, reconnaissance assets, and adjacent units.

docs.title: Key Spatial Functions
docs.text:
• Intelligence preparation of the battlefield (IPB): The S2, supported by the S3, analyses the terrain and enemy to produce a detailed picture of the battlespace. IPB identifies key terrain, enemy avenues of approach, and likely enemy positions. It is the spatial foundation for all planning.

  • Common operating picture: The staff maintains a shared visual representation of the battlespace. The COP shows the positions of friendly and enemy units, control measures, and key terrain. It must be updated continuously to remain accurate.

  • Control measures: The staff establishes control measures — boundaries, phase lines, objectives, and fire support coordination measures — that define the spatial framework for operations. Control measures enable subordinate commanders to operate freely within a coherent framework.

  • Terrain management: The staff allocates terrain to subordinate units based on the commander's intent. Each company is assigned an area of operations that provides the space it needs to accomplish its mission while maintaining mutual support with adjacent companies.

docs.title: The Battalion Staff's Temporal Problem
docs.text: The battalion staff manages time through the battle rhythm — the routine cycle of meetings, reports, and orders that synchronises the battalion's operations.

docs.title: Key Temporal Functions
docs.text:
• Synchronisation: The S3 coordinates the actions of companies, supporting weapons, and adjacent units to produce maximum combined effect at the right time. Synchronisation is the temporal equivalent of mutual support in space.

  • Decision cycle management: The staff manages the commander's decision cycle. The commander makes decisions at key points in the operation. The staff ensures that the commander has the information needed to make those decisions on time.

  • Reporting: The staff establishes reporting requirements that provide the commander with timely information without overwhelming the staff with unnecessary data. Reports must be frequent enough to be relevant but not so frequent that they create information overload.

  • Planning horizons: The staff manages multiple planning horizons simultaneously. Current operations are executed. Near-future operations are planned. Far-future operations are conceptualised. Each horizon requires different levels of detail and different staff actions.

docs.title: The OODA Loop at the Battalion Level
docs.text: At the battalion level, the OODA loop is a staff function, not an individual one. The staff processes information, develops options, and presents recommendations to the commander. The commander decides. The staff translates the decision into orders.

docs.title: Observe
docs.text: The battalion staff observes through multiple channels: company reports, intelligence feeds, reconnaissance assets, and information from higher headquarters. The challenge is to fuse this information into a coherent picture.

docs.title: Orient
docs.text: The staff orients by analysing the information and assessing its implications. Is the enemy acting as expected? Are companies where they should be? Is the situation developing according to plan? The orientation process is continuous and requires constant updating.

docs.title: Decide
docs.text: The commander decides, but the staff recommends. The S3 presents options with recommendations. The commander selects a course of action. The decision must be timely — too early risks acting on incomplete information; too late risks losing the initiative.

docs.title: Act
docs.text: The staff translates the commander's decision into orders. Orders must be clear, concise, and timely. They must include the commander's intent, the concept of operations, and specific tasks for each subordinate unit.

docs.title: The S2/S3 Relationship
docs.text:
The S2 (intelligence) and S3 (operations) relationship is the core of the battalion staff's space-time management. The S2 provides the spatial picture — where is the enemy, what is the terrain, what are the enemy's likely courses of action. The S3 provides the temporal picture — when will actions occur, how long will they take, what is the sequence of events.

Together, the S2 and S3 enable the commander to visualise the battlespace in four dimensions: three of space and one of time. This four-dimensional visualisation is the foundation of command at the battalion level.

docs.title: Space-Time and the Battalion Attack
docs.text:
The battalion attack is a complex space-time problem. The staff must:

  1. Plan: Develop a scheme of manoeuvre that places companies on objectives at the right time. Coordinate supporting fires. Establish control measures. Issue orders.

  2. Prepare: Move companies to the line of departure. Coordinate with adjacent units. Brief company commanders. Ensure all units understand the plan.

  3. Execute: Control the battalion's movement. Adjust the plan as the situation changes. Commit reserves at the right time and place.

  4. Consolidate: Secure objectives. Reorganise the battalion. Prepare for counterattack.

Each phase requires the staff to manage space and time simultaneously. The staff must ensure that companies are in the right place at the right time with the right support.

docs.title: Case Study — Operation Desert Storm: The Left Hook
docs.text:
"The greatest military victory in a generation, achieved through mastery of space and time." — Williamson Murray and Kevin Woods, The Iran-Iraq War

This case study examines the 1991 Gulf War's ground campaign, focusing on the operational-level mastery of space and time that enabled coalition forces to defeat the Iraqi army in 100 hours.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
On 2 August 1990, Iraq invaded Kuwait. The United States led a coalition of 35 nations to liberate Kuwait. The campaign had two phases:

  1. Desert Storm (17 January – 28 February 1991): A 38-day air campaign that destroyed Iraqi air defenses, command and control, and logistics.

  2. Desert Sabre (24 – 28 February 1991): A four-day ground campaign that liberated Kuwait and destroyed the Iraqi Republican Guard.

This case study focuses on the ground campaign and the operational maneuver known as the "Left Hook."

docs.title: The Operational Problem
docs.text:
The coalition faced a significant space-time problem. The Iraqi army occupied Kuwait and southern Iraq. The coalition could attack directly into Kuwait — a frontal assault against prepared defenses. Or it could maneuver around the Iraqi flank — a wide envelopment through the western desert.

The frontal assault was spatially direct but temporally costly. The Iraqis had months to prepare defenses: minefields, wire, fire trenches, and pre-registered artillery. A frontal assault would be slow and costly.

The envelopment was spatially complex but temporally advantageous. The western desert was largely undefended. A rapid maneuver through the desert could outflank the Iraqi army and cut its lines of retreat. But the maneuver required moving hundreds of thousands of troops and vehicles across hundreds of kilometers of desert in a matter of days.

docs.title: The Left Hook
docs.text: General Norman Schwarzkopf, the coalition commander, chose the envelopment. The plan had two elements:

docs.title: 1. The Direct Attack
docs.text: The U.S. Marine Corps and Arab coalition forces attacked directly into Kuwait. This attack fixed the Iraqi army in place. The Iraqis reinforced their defenses in Kuwait, weakening their western flank.

docs.title: 2. The Left Hook
docs.text:
The U.S. VII Corps and XVIII Airborne Corps executed a wide envelopment through the western desert. The corps moved west of Kuwait, then turned east to attack the Iraqi Republican Guard from the rear.

The Left Hook covered approximately 300 kilometers of desert. The corps moved at speeds of 40 to 80 kilometers per hour. The maneuver was completed in less than 48 hours.

docs.title: Spatial Factors
docs.text:
The Left Hook exploited a critical spatial gap in the Iraqi defense. The Iraqis had concentrated their forces in Kuwait and along the Saudi-Kuwait border. The western desert was undefended. The coalition exploited this gap by moving through terrain the Iraqians considered impassable.

The maneuver required precise navigation across featureless desert. The coalition used GPS (then in its early operational stages) and inertial navigation systems to maintain orientation. Without GPS, the Left Hook would have been impossible.

docs.title: Temporal Factors
docs.text:
The Left Hook was a race against time. The coalition had to complete the maneuver before the Iraqis detected the envelopment and redeployed their forces. The coalition used deception to mask the maneuver. The Marines' attack into Kuwait convinced the Iraqis that the main effort was frontal.

The corps moved continuously for 48 hours. Troops slept in vehicles. Maintenance was performed on the move. The tempo was relentless. The corps that arrived at the objective on time was the corps that won.

docs.title: Synchronisation
docs.text:
The Left Hook required precise synchronisation between the direct attack and the envelopment. The Marines had to fix the Iraqi army in place before the VII Corps and XVIII Airborne Corps completed the envelopment. If the Marines attacked too early, the Iraqis would have time to redeploy. If the Marines attacked too late, the envelopment would be exposed.

The synchronisation was achieved through a detailed timeline. The Marines attacked on 24 February at 0400. The VII Corps completed the envelopment on 25 February. The XVIII Airborne Corps cut the lines of retreat on 26 February. The Republican Guard was destroyed by 28 February.

docs.title: The Result
docs.text:
The ground campaign lasted 100 hours. The coalition destroyed 38 Iraqi divisions. Iraqi casualties exceeded 50,000. Coalition casualties were fewer than 500.

The Left Hook demonstrated the decisive advantage of operational-level space-time mastery. The coalition moved faster than the Iraqis could react. The coalition exploited spatial gaps the Iraqis did not know existed. The coalition synchronised its actions with precision the Iraqis could not match.

docs.title: 1. Tempo Is Decisive
docs.text: The coalition's tempo was overwhelming. The Iraqis could not comprehend the speed of the maneuver. By the time they understood what was happening, it was too late.

docs.title: 2. Space Must Be Exploited
docs.text: The western desert was a spatial gap. The coalition exploited it. The Iraqis assumed the desert was impassable. They were wrong.

docs.title: 3. Synchronisation Requires a Timeline
docs.text: The Left Hook succeeded because of a detailed timeline. Every element knew when to act. The timeline was the temporal framework for the operation.

docs.title: 4. Deception Masks Intent
docs.text: The Marines' attack into Kuwait convinced the Iraqis that the main effort was frontal. The Left Hook was masked until it was too late.

docs.title: 5. Technology Enables Maneuver
docs.text: GPS enabled navigation across featureless desert. Without GPS, the Left Hook would have been impossible. Technology compressed the space-time domain.

docs.title: Platoon Commander's Space-Time — Synchronising Intent Across the Battlespace
docs.text:
"The platoon leader must have a relatively complete knowledge of the terrain, and he must know as much as possible about the enemy." — FM 3-21.8, Infantry Platoon and Squad

The platoon commander operates at the tactical level where intent is translated into action. The platoon commander receives the company commander's intent and must achieve it through the coordinated action of multiple sections. This requires mastery of space and time at a higher level than the section commander.

This page discusses the space-time domain at the platoon and company level, relevant to lieutenants and captains.

docs.title: The Platoon Commander's Spatial Problem
docs.text: The platoon commander must visualise the battlespace in three dimensions. Where are the enemy? Where are my sections? Where is the terrain that affects the plan? Where are the boundaries between adjacent units?

docs.title: Key Spatial Tasks
docs.text:
The platoon commander performs several spatial tasks simultaneously:

  • Terrain analysis: Identifying key terrain, observation and fields of fire, cover and concealment, obstacles, and avenues of approach. The platoon commander uses OCOKA and METT-TC (Mission, Enemy, Terrain, Troops, Time, Civil Considerations) to analyse the ground.

  • Section positioning: Placing sections in positions that maximise their combat power while maintaining mutual support. The platoon commander must ensure that sections can support each other with fire and that no section is isolated.

  • Route selection: Choosing routes that balance speed with security. The fastest route may be the most dangerous. The safest route may be too slow. The platoon commander must select the route that achieves the intent in the time available.

  • Boundary management: Operating within the company's area of operations while coordinating with adjacent platoons. The platoon commander must be aware of boundaries to prevent fratricide and ensure seamless coordination.

docs.title: The Platoon Commander's Temporal Problem
docs.text: Time at the platoon level is measured in minutes and hours. The platoon commander must synchronise multiple actions in time.

docs.title: Key Temporal Tasks
docs.text:
• Timeline management: The platoon commander works backwards from the time of the attack or defence. When must sections be in position? When must supporting fires begin? When must the objective be seized? The platoon commander builds a timeline that accounts for movement, preparation, and execution.

  • Synchronisation: The platoon commander synchronises the actions of sections, supporting weapons, and adjacent units. Synchronisation ensures that all elements act at the right time to produce maximum combined effect. A section that arrives too early may be destroyed in isolation. A section that arrives too late may miss the window of opportunity.

  • Tempo control: The platoon commander controls the tempo of the platoon's operations. Tempo is not constant. It accelerates during the assault and slows during consolidation. The platoon commander must be able to change tempo quickly in response to the situation.

docs.title: The OODA Loop at the Platoon Level
docs.text: Boyd's OODA loop applies at the platoon level, but the cycle is more complex than at the section level. The platoon commander must process information from multiple sources: sections, the company commander, adjacent platoons, and supporting units.

docs.title: Observe
docs.text: The platoon commander observes through multiple channels: reports from section commanders, radio traffic, personal observation, and information from higher headquarters. The challenge is to filter relevant information from noise.

docs.title: Orient
docs.text: The platoon commander orients by matching new information with the existing understanding of the situation. Is the enemy as expected? Is the terrain as expected? Are sections where they should be? The orientation process is continuous and must be updated rapidly as new information arrives.

docs.title: Decide
docs.text: The platoon commander decides on a course of action. At the platoon level, decisions are more complex than at the section level. The platoon commander must consider the impact on multiple sections, supporting weapons, and the company plan. Decisions must be communicated clearly and quickly.

docs.title: Act
docs.text: The platoon commander acts by issuing orders to section commanders. The orders must be clear, concise, and timely. The platoon commander must ensure that sections understand not only what to do, but why — the intent behind the order.

docs.title: Synchronisation and the Platoon Sergeant
docs.text:
The platoon commander does not manage space and time alone. The platoon sergeant is the platoon commander's principal assistant for synchronisation. The platoon sergeant manages logistics, coordinates supporting weapons, and ensures that sections are in position on time.

The platoon commander and platoon sergeant form a two-person command team. The platoon commander focuses on the enemy and the mission. The platoon sergeant focuses on the troops and the timeline. Together, they ensure that the platoon operates as a cohesive unit in space and time.

docs.title: Space-Time and the Platoon Attack
docs.text:
The platoon attack is a space-time problem. The platoon commander must:

  1. Plan: Analyse the terrain, the enemy, and the time available. Develop a scheme of manoeuvre that places the platoon on the objective at the right time.

  2. Prepare: Move the platoon to the line of departure. Coordinate supporting fires. Brief section commanders. Ensure all sections understand the plan and the intent.

  3. Execute: Control the platoon's movement to the objective. Adjust the plan as the situation changes. Commit the assault at the right time and place.

  4. Consolidate: Secure the objective. Reorganise the platoon. Prepare for counterattack. The consolidation phase is often neglected but is critical to holding ground.

Each phase has spatial and temporal dimensions. The platoon commander must manage both simultaneously.

docs.title: Section Commander's Space-Time — Reading Ground, Time, and Intent
docs.text:
"Get there firstest with the mostest." — Confederate General Nathan Bedford Forrest

The section commander operates at the lowest level of military command. Decisions are immediate. The consequences are direct. There is no time for detailed analysis. The section commander must read the ground, understand time pressure, and act on intent.

This page discusses the space-time domain at the tactical level most relevant to junior leaders: the lance corporal and corporal commanding a fire team or section.

docs.title: Reading the Ground
docs.text: Terrain is the physical framework within which every engagement occurs. The section commander must read terrain quickly and accurately.

docs.title: Key Terrain Features
docs.text:
Terrain is analysed using the military mnemonic OCOKA:

  • Observation: Where can you see the enemy? Where can the enemy see you? Good observation enables effective fire and early warning. Poor observation creates surprise.

  • Cover and concealment: Cover protects from fire. Concealment hides from observation. The section commander must identify both and use them to protect the section.

  • Obstacles: Natural or artificial features that impede movement. Rivers, walls, minefields, wire. Obstacles can protect flanks or block routes of advance.

  • Key terrain: Any feature whose seizure, retention, or control provides a marked advantage to either side. A hilltop. A bridge. A road junction. Key terrain is the spatial focus of the battle.

  • Avenues of attack: Routes along which a force can move to reach its objective. The section commander must identify covered and concealed avenues that allow the section to close with the enemy.

docs.title: Ground and Movement
docs.text:
The section commander must calculate not merely the distance to an objective, but the time required to traverse that distance in the specific terrain. A kilometre of open ground takes minutes. A kilometre of dense vegetation takes longer. A kilometre under fire takes longest of all.

Ground also determines the formation the section adopts. Open terrain may allow a wide skirmish line. Jungle requires a single file. Urban terrain requires bounding overwatch between buildings.

docs.title: Understanding Time
docs.text: Time at the section level is measured in seconds and minutes. The section commander must understand three temporal factors:

docs.title: 1. Time Available
docs.text: How long before the section must be at the objective? How long before the enemy will arrive? How long before the supporting artillery lifts? The section commander works backwards from these deadlines to determine what is possible.

docs.title: 2. Time to Move
docs.text: The section commander must estimate movement time based on terrain, load, and conditions. A fit section moves at approximately four kilometres per hour on roads. This drops to two kilometres per hour cross-country and one kilometre per hour in dense vegetation. Under fire, movement is slower still.

docs.title: 3. Time to React
docs.text:
The most critical temporal factor. When contact occurs, the section commander must recognise the threat and issue orders within seconds. The faster the section reacts, the more likely it is to survive and win.

Boyd's OODA loop applies at the section level. The section that observes the enemy first, orients correctly, decides quickly, and acts decisively gains the initiative. The section that hesitates loses.

docs.title: Acting on Intent
docs.text:
The section commander receives orders from the platoon commander. These orders include the commander's intent — the purpose of the operation and the desired end state. The section commander must understand intent well enough to act when the plan changes.

Intent at the section level is simple. "Seize that hilltop." "Defend this position." "Provide covering fire for the platoon advance." The section commander must be able to achieve the intent even when communication fails or the situation changes.

This requires mission command at the lowest level. The platoon commander states the intent. The section commander decides how to achieve it. If the planned route is blocked, the section commander selects an alternative. If the enemy appears from an unexpected direction, the section commander reacts without waiting for orders.

docs.title: The Section Commander's Decision Cycle
docs.text:
The section commander's decision cycle is compressed. There is no time for detailed analysis. The cycle is:

  1. Observe: Detect the enemy. Identify terrain features. Note changes in the situation.

  2. Orient: Match what you see with what you know. Is this the expected enemy? Is this terrain as expected? Does this change the plan?

  3. Decide: Choose a course of action. The section commander has limited options: advance, defend, delay, or withdraw. The decision must be quick.

  4. Act: Issue fire orders. Direct movement. Control the section. The action must be immediate.

This cycle repeats continuously throughout the engagement. The section commander who cycles faster than the enemy section gains the advantage.

docs.title: Space-Time and the Junior Leader
docs.text:
The lance corporal does not plan campaigns. But the lance corporal must understand space and time at the most fundamental level. Where am I? Where is the enemy? Where is my objective? How long will it take to get there? How long do I have? What happens if I am late?

These questions are the foundation of tactical decision-making. The section commander who can answer them quickly and accurately is the section commander who wins.

docs.title: Exercise Design
docs.text: "Exercise design is the bridge between learning objectives and realistic decision-making. A well-designed exercise creates the conditions for commanders and staff to practice the art of command under controlled stress."

This section is part of the Strategos Telos wargaming library. It is intended to be generalizable to military exercise design practice worldwide.

docs.title: Commissioning and Initiation
docs.text: The exercise design process begins when the authority responsible for training identifies a need and issues a commissioning instruction or exercise directive. This document defines: - Exercise name and classification - Purpose and type - Aim and focus - Training and exercise objectives - Participating and supporting forces - Timeframe and locations - Key appointments - Resource allocation and constraints

docs.title: Commissioning Instruction
docs.text: The commissioning instruction serves as the tasking document that: - Mandates the exercise - Appoints an Exercise Director - Demarcates the objectives of the exercise - Provides the framework within which the exercise is to be designed - Stipulates the timeline for development and execution

docs.title: Exercise Specification Meeting
docs.text: Before an exercise is commissioned, the Officer Scheduling the Exercise conveys intent, guidelines, and objectives in a formal conference to the core planning group. This meeting: - Identifies key requirements and objectives - Serves as the framework for drafting the commissioning instruction or exercise directive - Defines the authority for all subsequent planning sessions

docs.title: Initial Planning Conference
docs.text: Once the concept has been developed, the Exercise Director issues an exercise warning order and convenes the Initial Planning Conference. The IPC: - Presents the approved concept to the full planning group - Creates decentralized work groups for detailed planning - Begins the translation of concept into executable plans

docs.title: Exercise Control Structure
docs.text:
A balanced control structure is essential. Too large a control element strains the budget; too small a structure creates safety and control risks.

Typical core elements: - Exercise Director — overall authority and final decisions - Exercise Control — scenario management, timing, and injects - Scenario Development Cell — narrative and scenario maintenance - Evaluation Cell — observation, assessment, and after-action review production - Simulation Control — simulation integration where applicable - Specialist Staff — safety, logistics, communications, medical - Real-Life Support — force protection, emergency response, administration

docs.title: Exercise Documentation
docs.text: Standard exercise documentation typically includes: - Commissioning instruction or exercise directive - Exercise concept paper - Exercise plan and exercise order - Narrative and scenario documents - MEL/MIL list and control matrix - Evaluation plan and after-action review guidance - Safety plan and real-life support annexes

docs.title: Exercise Types
docs.text:
Military exercises exist on a spectrum from study to live field execution.

Type Description Typical Use Study period / staff ride Paper-based or terrain walk-through; low resource Concept familiarization, doctrine review Map exercise / table-top exercise (TTX) Map or model-based decision-making; no troops Command-post training, staff coordination Tactical decision exercise / TDG Short timed decision vignettes; individual or small group Leader judgment drills, PME blocks Command post exercise (CPX) Headquarters-focused; simulated or real staff Staff procedures, C2 systems, decision-making Field training exercise (FTX) Live execution with troops and equipment Tactical proficiency, combined arms integration Computer-assisted exercise (CAX) Virtual, constructive, or live simulation integration Large-scale operations, joint/combined training Command field exercise (CFX) Hybrid CPX + limited live execution Command and control under semi-realistic conditions

docs.title: Planning and Development
docs.text: Concept development and detailed planning turn the commissioning instruction into an executable exercise plan.

docs.title: Concept Development Conference
docs.text:
The core planning team, usually led by the Exercise Director, develops the exercise concept. For complex exercises, this phase should begin 8 to 12 months before execution.

Key outputs: - Exercise concept paper - Preliminary control structure - Planning timeline - Initial exercise objectives and training objectives

The conference should function as a collective think tank. Small break-away groups may be permitted, but centralized planning should be encouraged to keep all planners aligned.

docs.title: Planning Conferences
docs.text: Conference Purpose Timing Initial Planning Conference (IPC) Present concept; create work groups; begin detailed planning 4–6 months before execution Main Planning Conference (MPC) Integrate work group outputs; finalize exercise plan and order 2–3 months before execution Final Planning Conference (FPC) Confirm readiness; review and update plan; issue final exercise order 2–4 weeks before execution

docs.title: Backward Planning
docs.text: All exercise planning should use backward planning from the execution date. Mark milestones for: - Concept development completion - Initial, main, and final planning conferences - Mobilization and force deployment - Rehearsals and validation events

docs.title: Objective Alignment
docs.text: Every element of the exercise — from narrative to injects to evaluation — should map directly to stated training objectives. Avoid adding activities that do not serve the exercise aim.

docs.title: Scenario Writing
docs.text: "A compelling scenario is paramount to the success of a wargame. If the scenario fails to engage the players, the wargame is likely to falter."

This section is part of the Strategos Telos wargaming library. It is intended to be generalizable to military wargaming and exercise design practice worldwide.

docs.title: What Is a Scenario?
docs.text: A scenario provides the context for decision-making and sets the stage for the wargame. It should include a compelling background, clear player objectives, defined relationships, available resources, and mechanisms for information updates.

docs.title: Scenario Background
docs.text: A well-crafted background increases scenario credibility and deters challenges. It should: - Establish the key actors in the wargame - Identify their general attitudes, intentions, and goals - Provide the political, economic, and social context - Explain the historical and strategic background that led to the situation

docs.title: Player Objectives
docs.text: Clearly defining what each player is attempting to achieve creates tension or conflict between key players. Objectives should be: - Specific and measurable - Potentially conflicting between sides - Aligned with the wargame's overall purpose

docs.title: Defined Relationships and Command Affiliations
docs.text: Establish the organizational structure or command relationship of all players: - Hierarchy of command within teams - Diplomatic relations between teams - Chain of command for orders and reporting

docs.title: Available Resources
docs.text: Resources at each player's disposal during the wargame: - Order of Battle (OOB) for military units - Equipment and weapons systems - Intelligence resources - Logistical capabilities - Financial and political capital

docs.title: Information Update Mechanisms
docs.text: How the scenario evolves and how information is shared: - Regular situation reports (SITREPs) - Intelligence updates - Unexpected developments or injects - Communication protocols and delays

docs.title: Scenario Writing Checklist
docs.text:
• Clear connection to wargame objectives
  • Credible background narrative
  • Defined player objectives with potential conflict
  • Complete order of battle for all sides
  • Terrain and environmental conditions specified
  • Information update mechanisms defined
  • Injects planned for key decision points
  • Cultural context incorporated
  • Scenario validated by subject matter experts

docs.title: The Scenario in the Wargame Cycle
docs.text:
Tasking → Design → Development → Testing → Rehearsal → Execution → Post-Game → Archival
                ↑                                                              |
                └──────────────── Scenario iteration and improvement ──────────┘

docs.title: Scenario Design Process
docs.text:
1. Understand the purpose — What analytical question is the wargame answering?
  2. Define the setting — Where and when does the scenario take place?
  3. Establish the actors — Who are the key players and what are their goals?
  4. Create the narrative — What sequence of events leads to the wargame's starting point?
  5. Set the conditions — What are the initial force dispositions, terrain, and weather?
  6. Design the injects — What events will disrupt and challenge player plans?
  7. Validate realism — Does the scenario reflect plausible real-world conditions?

docs.title: Scenario Robustness
docs.text:
A scenario should be robust enough to offer players latitude to make decisions about issues important to the sponsor, without being overly restrictive or permissive.

  • Overly restrictive: Players feel railroaded; exploration is limited
  • Overly permissive: Players lose focus; the wargame drifts from its objectives

docs.title: Inject Design
docs.text: Injects are unexpected developments that keep the scenario dynamic and realistic. Effective injects: - Are timed to challenge existing plans - Test player adaptability - Reflect real-world uncertainty and fog of war - Are plausible within the scenario's context

docs.title: Narrative Design
docs.text: A compelling scenario requires a narrative that resonates with players and aligns with their real-world experiences. The narrative should be credible and internally consistent, reflect the operational environment accurately, include human elements, and account for cultural context.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
1. Orientation — Introduce the operational environment, including geography, climate, infrastructure, and human terrain.
  2. Historical Background — Describe the strategic and operational background that explains how the situation developed. Identify the main actors, their motivations, and the conflict triggers.
  3. Escalation / Road to Crisis or War — Chronologically unpack recent events that led to the current situation. Show a clear increase in tension and the key incidents that pushed the situation toward conflict.
  4. Mission — State the military problem and the mission that brings the primary training audience into the situation. This may be a structured mission from higher headquarters or an unstructured problem that requires analysis and appreciation.

docs.title: Design Steps
docs.text:
1. Geographical placement — Choose real or fictional terrain. Prepare maps at appropriate scales.
  2. Identify conflict triggers — Select one or more political, social, economic, or military triggers that start the conflict.
  3. Identify main actors — Define each actor's aims, capabilities, power base, and threat potential.
  4. Conflict mapping — Plot incidents on a timeline or map to control tempo and escalation.
  5. Mission statement — Define the military mission that transitions from operational to tactical level.
  6. Supporting documents — Prepare orders, intelligence summaries, ROE, and logistics data.
  7. Draft the narrative — Write the full narrative, keeping it concise, accurate, and clear.

docs.title: Levels of War
docs.text:
The concept of "levels of war" guides the organisation and execution of military operations.

Level Focus Technical Understanding and improving technical aspects of equipment operation Low-Tactical Training individual soldiers or small units High-Tactical Training commanders to control larger units (battalions, regiments) Operational Planning and coordination of large-scale military operations Military Strategic High-level military planning and decision-making National Strategic Broader implications of military actions on national security and policy Regional/Global Strategic Impacts on regional stability or global peace

docs.title: Beyond Conflict
docs.text:
Military simulation and wargaming also apply to: - Management — organisational decision-making - Business — competitive strategy - Competition — Fittest Soldier-type events for morale and mental fitness

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: Future Trends
docs.text: Military simulation and wargaming are being reshaped by technology trends, particularly AI, ML, and big data analytics.

docs.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
docs.text:
AI-powered agents can simulate enemy forces, creating dynamic and unpredictable scenarios that mirror real-world combat uncertainties.

Benefits: - Enhanced realism and complexity - Dynamic scenario generation - Real-time adaptation to trainee actions

Risks: - Overreliance on technology - Neglect of human intuition - Vulnerability to cyber threats - Limited by training data quality and biases

docs.title: Big Data Analytics
docs.text:
Integration of sensor data, social media, and other sources to create comprehensive battlefield representations.

Benefits: - More nuanced operational environment understanding - Dynamic scenario updating

Risks: - Data security and privacy concerns - Challenge of managing vast information volumes

docs.title: Cloud Computing
docs.text:
Seamless integration of systems and platforms; facilitates data sharing across command levels.

Benefits: - Increased flexibility and accessibility - Cross-level coordination

Risks: - Internet connectivity dependence - Cloud service disruption vulnerability

docs.title: Virtual and Augmented Reality
docs.text:
Immersion in complex operational environments or emergency scenarios.

Benefits: - Safe yet realistic training - Enhanced spatial understanding

Risks: - Costly implementation - Cannot fully replicate physical and psychological stresses of real operations

docs.title: Cybersecurity
docs.text:
As simulations become more digital, cybersecurity becomes critical.

Requirements: - Robust security protocols for simulation data integrity - Ongoing maintenance and updates - Personnel training in cybersecurity practices

docs.title: Personalized Training
docs.text:
AI-powered simulations tailored to individual soldiers' needs and abilities.

Consideration: AI systems are only as good as their training data. Biased or incomplete data produces flawed recommendations.

docs.title: More Realistic Scenarios
docs.text:
AI creates dynamic scenarios adapting in real-time to trainee actions.

Consideration: No simulation can fully replicate the unpredictability and chaos of real combat. Must complement with live exercises.

docs.title: Increased Focus on Decision-Making
docs.text:
Real-time feedback and analysis to develop decision-making abilities.

Consideration: Human judgement of experienced personnel must always play a central role — not over-reliance on AI feedback.

docs.title: Integration of Human Factors
docs.text:
Incorporating fatigue, stress, and psychological considerations.

Ethical consideration: Simulating high-stress situations may have negative psychological impacts. Appropriate safeguards and support systems are required.

docs.title: Enhanced Decision-Making
docs.text:
• Real-time data and analysis for strategic planning
  • Risk: Overreliance leading to complacency and reduced critical thinking

docs.title: Increased Efficiency
docs.text:
• Reduced time and resources for training
  • Risk: Simulations may not replicate real combat pressures

docs.title: Improved Situational Awareness
docs.text:
• Comprehensive battlefield view from multiple data sources
  • Risk: Data quality directly affects effectiveness

docs.title: Enhanced Collaboration
docs.text:
• Real-time data enabling better communication and coordination
  • Risk: Security concerns with sensitive data sharing; information overload

docs.title: Overreliance on New Technologies
docs.text:
Emerging technologies like AI, VR, and AR offer significant advantages, but overreliance leads to: - Neglect of vital military training aspects - Inability to replicate human intuition critical to battlefield decisions - Substantial upfront investment burden for constrained defence budgets

Technology can be a force multiplier for countries that can afford and sustain it. It becomes a burdensome millstone for everyone else.

docs.title: Neglect of Traditional Methods
docs.text: Conceptual wargaming fosters critical thinking, creativity, and adaptability. Traditional methods remain effective and should not be disregarded.

docs.title: Misplaced Focus
docs.text: The primary purpose is not to win, but to learn. Focus on victory rather than learning undermines the wargame's purpose.

docs.title: Poorly Understood Objectives
docs.text: If objectives are not thoroughly understood by participants, the simulation fails to yield useful results.

docs.title: Ignorance of Military Simulation and Wargaming
docs.text: Lack of understanding by key personnel affects realism and usefulness. Remedy through increased awareness, understanding, and communication of benefits.

docs.title: Cultural Context and the Lie of Reasonable Actors
docs.text:
From a South African perspective, the behaviour of Actor A may seem unreasonable, but it is very rational within that actor's cultural context. This can be mitigated by letting participants become specialized in the relevant culture.

Source: Wargaming and Military Simulation for the SANDF, TRG COMD/R/103/6, May 2025, Capt P.A.R. Malan.

docs.title: Generations of Wargames
docs.text: Wargames are classified into generations based on their complexity, modelling fidelity, and underlying technology.

docs.title: First-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Abstract competition where outcomes are determined primarily by player decisions
  • No sophisticated models of reality
  • Turn-based; no dimension of time
  • Examples: Chess, Go, Senet

docs.title: Second-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Underlying model representative of actual time and space
  • Depicts combat, movement, attrition, logistics
  • Accurate scaled terrain and distances
  • Time incorporated — simultaneous or real-time decisions
  • Examples: Kriegsspiel, Flames of War, board wargames

docs.title: Third-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Highly detailed and realistic models simulating system-vs-system interaction
  • Incorporates computer systems and software
  • Can simulate large-scale operations with real-world data
  • Models complex interactions among various factors

Current limitation: No software exists that can be considered a full-fledged third-generation wargame. It is physically impossible to incorporate all possible systems and elements of power. Current "third-generation" products are second-generation wargames with additional features.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Represents entire military systems
  • Examines almost all dimensions of conflict
  • Focus on effects, effects-based outcomes, and synergy of systems
  • Forces go beyond military to include NGOs, civilians, journalists, police

docs.title: Fourth-Generation Wargames
docs.text:
• Move beyond war and conflict to include peace as a plausible path to victory
  • Blend politics, culture, religion, mass media, and global information flows with combat
  • Designed for the complexities of modern warfare and fourth-generation warfare

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
• Integration of AI, ML, and advanced technology
  • Dynamic and adaptive scenarios
  • Advanced analytics and feedback
  • Interdisciplinary approach (politics, religion, culture, media)
  • Focus on peaceful outcomes — peace as a desirable and plausible outcome
  • Dependent on current technical trends
